results.question: Ari has searched their library this turn with [Bog Glider]. During their end step, Nico casts [Mission Briefing]. Can they use it to cast [Archive Trap] from their graveyard for free?
results.text:
Yes. Nico may use Mission Briefing to cast Archive Trap from Nico’s graveyard and may pay {0} rather than Archive Trap’s mana cost, because Ari’s earlier search with Bog Glider counts as “an opponent searched their library this turn” for Archive Trap’s trap condition and Mission Briefing allows Nico to cast the chosen instant or sorcery from the graveyard this turn.

Reasoning and rules applied
- Define “search”: A spell or ability causes a player to search their library only if it specifically contains the word “search” in its text; Bog Glider’s ability says “Search your library…,” so Ari’s use of Bog Glider earlier this turn was a search and therefore counts as a library search this turn ([Archive Trap ruling #6]; Bog Glider). 
- Mission Briefing lets its controller cast a chosen instant or sorcery from their graveyard “this turn,” so Nico is allowed to begin to cast Archive Trap from Nico’s graveyard this turn (Mission Briefing; [Mission Briefing ruling #3]; see rule 601.3e about being allowed to cast a spell). 
- Archive Trap’s trap alternative cost reads “If an opponent searched their library this turn, you may pay {0} rather than pay this spell’s mana cost.” Archive Trap’s rules clarify that the trap condition checks only whether an opponent searched their library this turn (not whether they found anything), so Ari’s search with Bog Glider satisfies that condition for Nico if Ari is an opponent of Nico ([Archive Trap ruling #5]; [Archive Trap ruling #6]; Archive Trap). 
- Alternative costs are applied when a spell is cast; casting a spell for its alternative (trap) cost follows the normal rules for alternative costs and determining total cost (rules 118.9b and 601.2f). Therefore Nico may choose to pay {0} as Archive Trap’s cost when casting it from the graveyard this turn. 
- Note: You may instead cast Archive Trap for its normal mana cost if you prefer ([Archive Trap ruling #4]).

Multiplayer note: This answer assumes Ari is an opponent of Nico. In a multiplayer game, Archive Trap’s trap condition is satisfied only if any opponent of Nico searched their library this turn; if Ari is not an opponent of Nico, Ari’s search would not meet Archive Trap’s condition for Nico ([Archive Trap ruling #5]).

results.question: In a game of Two-Headed Giant, Antonio activates the last loyalty ability of [Chandra, Hope's Beacon] with X=1. Could they target both Nico and Noah?
results.text:
Yes. Antonio may target both Nico and Noah with Chandra, Hope's Beacon’s −X ability when X = 1, choosing them as the two targets; Chandra, Hope's Beacon will deal 1 damage to Nico and 1 damage to Noah. 

Reasoning and definitions (using only the provided rules): Chandra, Hope's Beacon’s −X ability reads, in part, “Chandra deals X damage to each of up to two targets,” so with X = 1 it deals 1 damage to each of up to two targets (Chandra, Hope's Beacon). Two-Headed Giant is played with two teams of two players each (rule 810.1), so Nico and Noah can be the two distinct players on the opposing team. Damage, loss of life, and gaining life happen to each player individually and then the result is applied to the team’s shared life total (rule 810.9d). Therefore, if Antonio targets Nico and Noah, Nico loses 1 life and Noah loses 1 life individually, and the opposing team’s shared life total is reduced by 2 as a result. 

Assumption: this answer assumes Nico and Noah are legal targets for Chandra, Hope's Beacon’s ability at the time it’s activated (no provided rule text here prohibits targeting two different players on the same team).

results.question: Avalyn has no cards in their library and controls a [Keranos, God of Storms]. What happens at the beginning of their draw step?
results.text:
Avalyn attempts to draw for their draw step, can’t because their library is empty, and will lose the game the next time a player would receive priority; Keranos, God of Storms’s reveal-and-trigger ability does not do anything because there was no card drawn to reveal. 

Reasoning and definitions: A “state-based action” is a game action that happens automatically whenever certain conditions are met and doesn’t use the stack [704.1]. The draw step’s first turn-based action is that the active player draws a card [504.1]; turn-based actions are performed when a step begins before state-based actions are checked [703.3]. If a player attempts to draw a card from a library with no cards in it, that player will lose the game the next time a player would receive priority (this is handled as a state-based action) [121.4, 704.5b]. After the turn-based draw action is performed and the game would next give out priority, state-based actions are checked and performed, causing Avalyn to lose at that time [704.3, 117.5]. 

Keranos, God of Storms’s text instructs you to reveal the first card you draw on each of your turns and creates effects based on what is revealed; because no card was drawn there is nothing to reveal and none of those reveal-triggered effects occur (see Keranos, God of Storms) [Keranos, God of Storms]. For reference, if a card were revealed and it were a land, Keranos, God of Storms’s ruling notes that would cause you to draw another card, but that is irrelevant here because no draw occurred [Keranos, God of Storms ruling #9].

results.question: Abdullah casts [Telemin Performance] targeting Nico. In response, Nico casts [Veil of Summer]. Abdullah responds with their own Veil of Summer. What happens?
results.text:
Direct answer: I can’t fully say whether Telemin Performance still affects Nico after Nico’s Veil of Summer resolves because the provided rules don’t include the rule that says what happens when a spell’s target becomes an illegal target between casting and resolution.

What we can say from the provided materials (assumptions: normal timing; all casts are legal):
- Abdullah casts Telemin Performance; putting it on the stack is casting a spell (see rule [601.2a]) so Telemin Performance is the bottom object of the three on the stack. (Card: Telemin Performance.)
- Nico casts Veil of Summer in response; that puts Nico’s Veil of Summer on the stack above Telemin Performance. (Card: Veil of Summer.)
- Abdullah casts Veil of Summer in response; Abdullah’s Veil of Summer becomes the topmost object on the stack. (Rule [601.2a].)
- Resolution order: topmost resolves first, so Abdullah’s Veil of Summer resolves first. Veil of Summer has no effect until it resolves ([Veil of Summer ruling #1]). Abdullah’s Veil of Summer therefore does not draw (Nico has not cast a blue or black spell), but it does give Abdullah “spells you control can’t be countered this turn” and gives Abdullah hexproof from blue and black until end of turn (Card: Veil of Summer). Because of [Veil of Summer ruling #2], that “spells you control can’t be countered this turn” protection will apply if a counterspell later resolves against Telemin Performance (i.e., it retroactively prevents the spell from being countered when the counterspell resolves).
- Nico’s Veil of Summer then resolves. Because Abdullah already cast Telemin Performance this turn (Telemin Performance is a blue spell), Nico will draw a card as Nico’s Veil resolves (Card: Veil of Summer; Card: Telemin Performance). Nico’s Veil also gives Nico and permanents Nico controls hexproof from blue and from black until end of turn; the parenthetical on Veil of Summer’s text explains that means “You and they can’t be the targets of blue or black spells or abilities your opponents control.” (Card: Veil of Summer.)

What is missing from the provided rules: the exact rule that governs what happens when a spell’s chosen target becomes an illegal target after the spell was cast but before it resolves (the rule that says whether the spell’s effects that target that object do nothing, or whether the spell is countered, or other outcome). Because that rule (and any ruling applying hexproof gained after a spell was cast to an already-chosen target) is not in the provided context, I cannot determine from the given material whether Telemin Performance’s targeting of Nico becomes illegal when Nico’s Veil resolves and, if it becomes illegal, what the results on resolution of Telemin Performance are.

If you provide the rule that describes what happens to spells with illegal targets at resolution (or an authoritative ruling about gaining hexproof after a spell has targeted you), I can finish the interaction precisely.

results.question: Athena controls [Teferi, Time Raveler] and Nicholas flashes in [The Wandering Emperor] on Athena's turn. Can Nicholas activate its abilities this turn?
results.text:
Yes. Nicholas may activate one loyalty ability of The Wandering Emperor this turn (but only one), and he may do so at instant timing whenever he has priority and the stack is empty; Teferi, Time Raveler’s restriction on when opponents can cast spells does not prevent activating The Wandering Emperor’s loyalty abilities.

Reasoning: A “loyalty ability” is an activated ability with a loyalty symbol in its cost (see rule 606.2 / 209.2). Normally loyalty abilities may be activated only during a main phase of their controller’s turn when the stack is empty (see rule 606.3). The Wandering Emperor’s text “As long as The Wandering Emperor entered this turn, you may activate her loyalty abilities any time you could cast an instant” is an activation instruction that changes when those loyalty abilities may be activated; activated-ability timing instructions function as instructions that must be followed while activating the ability (see rule 602.1b) and wording that refers to instant timing is applied as described for activated abilities that read like instant timing (see rule 602.5e). That lets Nicholas activate The Wandering Emperor’s loyalty abilities on Athena’s turn at instant timing, subject to the normal requirement that he have priority (see rule 117.1b) and that the stack be empty as required when activating loyalty abilities (see rule 606.3). In addition, The Wandering Emperor’s ruling confirms you may still only activate one of The Wandering Emperor’s loyalty abilities on the turn she entered the battlefield (The Wandering Emperor ruling #0).

Teferi, Time Raveler’s printed ability restricts when each opponent can cast spells (Teferi, Time Raveler card text). That restriction affects casting spells; it doesn’t say opponents can’t activate abilities. The separate ruling about Teferi’s interaction with permissions to cast as though a spell had flash clarifies how Teferi’s casting restriction interacts with permissions to cast spells as though they had flash (Teferi, Time Raveler ruling #0). Because The Wandering Emperor’s permission is about activating loyalty abilities (not about casting a spell), Teferi, Time Raveler’s casting-only restriction doesn’t stop Nicholas from activating The Wandering Emperor’s loyalty abilities.

Assumption and timing note: I assume Nicholas flashed The Wandering Emperor onto the battlefield this turn and that he hasn’t already activated one of The Wandering Emperor’s loyalty abilities this turn. If Nicholas had already activated one of The Wandering Emperor’s loyalty abilities this turn, he couldn’t activate another (see The Wandering Emperor ruling #0 and rule 606.3).

results.question: In a Two-Headed Giant game, how much life does each team begin the game with?
results.text:
Each team begins a Two-Headed Giant game with a shared life total of 30 life. (See rules [810.4] and [810.1].)

Definition and brief explanation: A Two-Headed Giant game is the multiplayer variant played with two teams of two players each ([810.1]). In that variant each team has a shared life total rather than individual life totals, and that shared life total starts at 30 life ([810.4]). Damage, loss of life, and gaining life happen to each player individually and are then applied to the team’s shared life total ([810.9]).

Note about larger-team variants: If a team has more than two players (Three-Headed Giant, Four-Headed Giant, etc.), each player beyond the second increases that team’s starting life total by 15 ([810.11]).

results.question: Alexis would like to choose colorless for [Regicide]. Can they?
results.text: No. Alexis can’t choose colorless for Regicide. Regicide’s drafting instruction asks players to “choose a color,” and when a player is asked to choose a color they must choose one of the five colors (white, blue, black, red, or green) [105.4]; the five colors are white, blue, black, red, and green [105.1]. “Colorless” is not a color and so cannot be chosen in that situation [105.4].

results.question: Alfonso controls [Cyclops of One-Eyed Pass] equipped with [Glaive of the Guildpact] and no Gates. Does it have vigilance and menace?
results.text: Yes — Cyclops of One-Eyed Pass has vigilance and menace while equipped with Glaive of the Guildpact, even though Alfonso controls no Gates. The equipped creature gains those keyword abilities because Glaive of the Guildpact’s effect grants vigilance and menace, and the card’s ruling explicitly states the equipped creature has vigilance and menace even if you control no Gates. Vigilance means attacking doesn’t cause a creature with vigilance to tap (rule 702.20b). Menace means a creature with menace can’t be blocked except by two or more creatures (rule 702.111b).

results.question: Ainsley casts [Tandem Takedown], granting their two [Devoted Hero] +1/+0. Can each Devoted Hero deal damage to a different one of Nolan's creatures?
results.text: No. Both Devoted Hero must deal their damage to the same chosen target; you can’t have each Devoted Hero deal damage to a different one of Nolan's creatures. Reasoning: When Ainsley cast Tandem Takedown, Ainsley chose up to two target creatures they control as the spell’s first set of targets and then chose the spell’s final damage target as part of casting (see rule [601.2a]). The phrase “up to two target creatures you control” is a single instance of the word “target” that can refer to two distinct creatures, so the two chosen Devoted Hero must be different legal targets for that instance ([115.3], [601.2a]). Tandem Takedown’s damage recipient is a single, separate target (the “last target” named in the card’s rulings), so both of the chosen Devoted Hero deal their damage to that same single target as the spell resolves. The official rulings for Tandem Takedown confirm this: if one of the first two targets is illegal as Tandem Takedown resolves, the other still gets +1/+0 and then deals damage to the single last target ([Tandem Takedown ruling #0]); if the last target is illegal as Tandem Takedown resolves (or if both of the first targets are illegal), nothing deals or is dealt damage ([Tandem Takedown ruling #1]).

results.question: Aaden has 3 [Witch's Familiar] in their graveyard and casts [Izoni, Thousand-Eyed]. After it enters the battlefield but before its trigger resolves, Nyla activates [Sentinel Totem] to exile all cards from Aaden's graveyard. When Izoni, Thousand-Eyed's ability resolves, how many tokens will be created?
results.text: Zero tokens will be created. When Izoni, Thousand-Eyed’s undergrowth ability resolves it looks at the number of creature cards in Aaden’s graveyard at that time and creates that many tokens; because Nyla’s Sentinel Totem activation exiled all graveyards before the ability resolved, there are 0 Witch's Familiar in Aaden’s graveyard, so 0 1/1 black and green Insect tokens are created. This follows the rule that an effect that requires information from the game (such as “the number of creature cards in your graveyard”) determines that information when the effect is applied (when the ability resolves) (see 608.2h), and the card-specific ruling for Izoni, Thousand-Eyed confirms that actions taken while the undergrowth ability is on the stack (for example, activating Izoni, Thousand-Eyed’s other ability) can change the number of tokens created (Izoni, Thousand-Eyed ruling #0). I’m assuming Sentinel Totem’s activated ability resolved before Izoni, Thousand-Eyed’s triggered ability resolved; if Sentinel Totem’s ability had not resolved, the number of tokens would be based on the graveyard’s contents at resolution (in your original situation that would have been three Witch's Familiar).

results.question: Atlas casts [Piracy] and would like to tap all of Nicole's lands but not cast any spells. Can Atlas do this?
results.text:
Yes. After Piracy resolves, Atlas may tap lands Nicole controls for mana and is not required to cast any spells with that mana; however, any mana produced that way may be spent only to cast spells this turn.

Reasoning and definitions (assumption: Piracy has resolved):
- "Tap lands you don't control for mana" means Atlas is allowed to activate the lands Nicole controls for their mana (i.e., tap those lands to add mana to Atlas’s mana) for the duration of the effect provided by Piracy. This permission comes from Piracy’s continuous effect (Piracy).
- Activating a mana ability is optional — a player isn’t required to activate mana abilities or to spend mana (see rule 118.3c). Therefore Atlas may choose to tap Nicole’s lands and then do nothing further instead of casting spells.
- The restriction printed on Piracy, "Spend this mana only to cast spells," limits what those particular mana can be spent on; it doesn’t force Atlas to spend the mana immediately or at all (Piracy).
- Atlas can do this only once Piracy has finished resolving and its effect is in place (assumption noted). While a spell or ability is resolving, special rules govern when mana abilities may be activated; see rule 608.2g and note that resolving objects finish their resolution as described in rule 608.2n.

If you meant Atlas attempting to tap Nicole’s lands before Piracy resolves, that would not work — the permission from Piracy exists only after Piracy’s resolution (assumption stated above).

results.question: Annie controls [Heliod, Sun-Crowned] and casts [Essence Feed]. Can they choose to put Heliod, Sun-Crowned's +1/+1 counter on one of the tokens created by Essence Feed?
results.text:
Yes. When Essence Feed resolves, you can put Heliod, Sun-Crowned’s +1/+1 counter on one of the Eldrazi Spawn tokens created by Essence Feed.

Reasoning: A triggered ability is an ability with a trigger condition and an effect; Heliod, Sun-Crowned’s ability is a triggered ability that triggers “Whenever you gain life” (see [603.1a]). Essence Feed’s resolution causes you to gain 3 life and creates three 0/1 Eldrazi Spawn creature tokens (Essence Feed). The life-gain event from Essence Feed causes Heliod, Sun-Crowned’s triggered ability to trigger once for that life-gaining event (Heliod, Sun-Crowned ruling #10). Because the tokens are created as part of the same resolving effect of Essence Feed, they will be on the battlefield by the time triggered abilities from that event are put on the stack, so Heliod, Sun-Crowned’s triggered ability can target one of those tokens and, as that triggered ability resolves, put a +1/+1 counter on it.

Timing assumption: This answer assumes the life gain and token creation from Essence Feed are part of the same resolving effect (the ordinary reading of Essence Feed’s text). If, contrary to that reading, the life gain happened entirely before the tokens were created, Heliod, Sun-Crowned’s trigger would still trigger when you gained life but you could only target creatures or enchantments that existed at the time the trigger was put on the stack; tokens created later would not be available to be targeted by that trigger.

results.question: Aleah casts [Clash of Titans], can Aleah choose Nixon's [Storm Crow] for both targets?
results.text:
No — Aleah can’t pick Nixon’s Storm Crow for both targets. Clash of Titans’s text is “Target creature fights another target creature,” so the spell’s second target must be a different creature than the first. 

Reasoning (short): A “target” is an object or player chosen for a spell or ability as it’s put on the stack [115.1]. The general rule about choosing the same object for multiple instances of the word “target” is in [115.3], but Clash of Titans’s printed wording includes the word “another,” which is part of the spell’s targeting criteria and therefore requires the second chosen creature to be a different creature than the first (the card’s own text governs how its targets are chosen). Clash of Titans can target two creatures you control, but they must be two different creatures [Clash of Titans ruling #0]. If either chosen target is illegal as Clash of Titans tries to resolve, neither creature deals or is dealt damage by that spell [Clash of Titans ruling #1].

Assumption: I’m assuming the usual timing where targets are chosen as part of casting the spell; if targets become illegal before resolution, see the ruling above about resolution.

results.question: Alejandro controls [Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider] and two [Blight Mamba]s. If Alejandro deals combat damage with both Blight Mambas, how many poison counters will Nico get?
results.text:
Nico gets four poison counters.

Why: Each Blight Mamba has infect, so when each Blight Mamba deals 1 combat damage to Nico, that damage causes Alejandro (the controller of those sources) to give Nico one poison counter per point of infect damage instead of causing loss of life ([702.90b], [120.3]). Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider’s ability says that if Alejandro would put one or more counters on a player, he puts twice that many of each of those kinds of counters on that player instead; because Alejandro is the one giving the poison counters, Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider’s doubling applies ([Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider], [Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider ruling #0]). Each 1-point infect event therefore becomes 2 poison counters, and with two Blight Mambas dealing damage simultaneously Nico gets 2 + 2 = 4 poison counters. The replacement effect doesn’t apply repeatedly to create more than double ([614.5]).

results.question: Andre casts [Abrupt Decay] targeting Nico's 5/5 Horse creature token, then responds by targeting it with [Arcane Denial]. What happens?
results.text:
Arcane Denial resolves but cannot counter Abrupt Decay; Abrupt Decay remains on the stack and will later check whether its target (Nico’s 5/5 Horse creature token) is still a legal target and, if so, will destroy it. Whether Abrupt Decay actually destroys the Horse depends on whether the Horse meets Abrupt Decay’s targeting requirement (a nonland permanent with mana value 3 or less) at the moment Abrupt Decay resolves — the provided rules don’t say what the Horse’s mana value is, so that part can’t be decided from the given material.

Reasoning and relevant rules (assumptions stated):
- Andre cast Abrupt Decay targeting Nico’s 5/5 Horse creature token; Nico then cast Arcane Denial targeting Abrupt Decay. Arcane Denial’s effect is to counter target spell (Arcane Denial card text).  
- Arcane Denial resolves: per Abrupt Decay’s ruling, a spell or ability that would counter Abrupt Decay can still target it, but “Abrupt Decay” can’t be countered, so the countering part of Arcane Denial won’t counter Abrupt Decay; any other effects of Arcane Denial still happen (for example, the delayed card draws) ([Abrupt Decay ruling #1]; Arcane Denial).  
- After Arcane Denial resolves, Abrupt Decay remains on the stack. When a permanent spell is resolving, it checks whether its target is still legal as described in rule 608.2b; if the target is illegal, the spell doesn’t resolve and is put into its owner’s graveyard ([608.3b]; [608.2b]).  
- “Illegal Target” is defined as a target that no longer exists or no longer meets the specifications stated by the spell or ability that’s targeting it (see rule 608.2b) ([Illegal Target]; [608.2b]). Abrupt Decay’s stated target specification is “target nonland permanent with mana value 3 or less” (Abrupt Decay).  
- The provided rules do say only permanents are legal targets unless otherwise specified ([115.2]), so a creature token on the battlefield is an object that can be targeted; but the provided material does not define what mana value such a token has, so it’s impossible to tell from the given rules whether the 5/5 Horse meets Abrupt Decay’s “mana value 3 or less” requirement at resolution.

If you assume the 5/5 Horse’s mana value is 3 or less, then Abrupt Decay will resolve and destroy Nico’s 5/5 Horse creature token. If you assume the 5/5 Horse’s mana value is greater than 3 (or the Horse otherwise fails the “mana value 3 or less” requirement) at Abrupt Decay’s resolution, Abrupt Decay will be removed from the stack and put into its owner’s graveyard without destroying the Horse. The answer depends on the missing rule that defines a token’s mana value (or otherwise determines whether the token meets Abrupt Decay’s mana-value condition).

results.question: Arabella controls [Yixlid Jailer] and casts [Ever After] targeting [Dearly Departed] and [Fugitive Wizard]. Will Fugitive Wizard enter with a +1/+1 counter?
results.text: No. Fugitive Wizard will not enter with a +1/+1 counter. Reasoning: Ever After returns Dearly Departed and Fugitive Wizard from the graveyard to the battlefield. Dearly Departed’s text creates a static ability that, while Dearly Departed is in your graveyard, would make each Human creature you control enter with an additional +1/+1 counter. However, Yixlid Jailer’s text makes cards in graveyards lose all abilities, so Dearly Departed has no such static ability while it’s in the graveyard and therefore creates no continuous effect to give creatures extra counters as they enter. Because that continuous effect is absent when Ever After returns the cards, Fugitive Wizard will enter normally (Ever After will make the returned creatures black Zombies in addition to their other colors and types, so Fugitive Wizard will be a Human Wizard and a Zombie on the battlefield), but it will not get a +1/+1 counter from Dearly Departed. Assumption: Ever After resolves and returns both cards from the graveyard as written; nothing else relevant changes between that moment and the creatures’ actual entering the battlefield.

results.question: Nicholas controls [Solitary Confinement]. Addilyn attacks with [Ranger of Eos] and casts [Skullcrack] targeting themselves. Does Nicholas lose life?
results.text:
Yes — assuming Skullcrack resolves before combat damage is dealt, Nicholas will lose life. Skullcrack’s “Damage can’t be prevented this turn” effect makes damage prevention impossible, so Solitary Confinement’s prevention won’t stop the combat damage; the damage is dealt and Nicholas’s life total is reduced accordingly.

Reasoning and definitions (assumption: Skullcrack resolves before combat damage is dealt; if Skullcrack resolves after the damage event is processed, the damage would already have been prevented by Solitary Confinement and Nicholas would not lose that damage):

- A prevention effect is an effect that watches for a damage event and completely or partially prevents that damage (definition: prevention effect; see rule 615.1). Solitary Confinement’s text and ruling state that Solitary Confinement prevents all damage that would be dealt to you (Solitary Confinement; Solitary Confinement ruling #1). 
- Skullcrack’s text says “Damage can’t be prevented this turn” (Skullcrack). An effect that states that something can’t happen (for example, “damage can’t be prevented”) is of the type described in rule 614.17c; those effects mean the event can’t happen and other replacement or prevention effects can’t modify or replace that event (614.17c). 
- Because Skullcrack makes prevention impossible, Solitary Confinement’s prevention effect can’t prevent the upcoming damage (615.1; 614.17c; Skullcrack). 
- When damage is dealt to a player by a source without infect, that player loses that much life (120.3a), and the player’s life total is adjusted accordingly (119.3). Therefore Nicholas takes the damage and loses life.

If instead Skullcrack resolves after combat damage was already processed and prevented by Solitary Confinement, Skullcrack’s inability-to-prevent effect can’t retroactively un-prevent that already-processed damage; in that timing Nicholas would not lose life from that already-processed damage.

results.question: Amina attacks with [Retaliation]. Nico declares no blocks and then casts [Curtain of Light] targeting Retaliation. Does Retaliation trigger?
results.text:
No — Retaliation’s granted ability does not trigger. Curtain of Light makes the attacking creature become blocked without causing any creature to become a blocking creature, and Retaliation’s ability requires the creature to “become blocked by a creature.”

Reasoning and definitions (short):
- “Becomes blocked” / “blocked creature”: An attacking creature becomes a blocked creature when one or more creatures are declared as blockers for it, and it remains blocked unless removed from combat or an effect changes that (rule 509.1h).
- “Becomes blocked by a creature”: An ability that triggers when a creature becomes blocked by a creature requires a creature to become a blocking creature for that attacker at the moment the blocker is declared (rule 509.3f).
- Curtain of Light’s text and rulings: Curtain of Light’s effect is “Target unblocked attacking creature becomes blocked,” and it can be cast after blockers are declared; Curtain of Light does cause “becomes blocked” events that trigger abilities that care only about “becomes blocked” (for example, it does trigger bushido abilities) ([Curtain of Light ruling #1], [Curtain of Light ruling #2]).
- Trigger condition check: A triggered ability only triggers if its trigger event actually occurs (rule 603.2g). Because no creature actually became a blocking creature when Curtain of Light resolved, the specific event “this creature becomes blocked by a creature” did not occur, so the ability granted by Retaliation (“Whenever this creature becomes blocked by a creature, this creature gets +1/+1 until end of turn.”) does not trigger (Retaliation; 509.3f; 509.1h; 603.2g).

Assumption and alternative timing: This answer assumes the sequence you described (Nico declares no blockers, then casts and resolves Curtain of Light during combat after blockers are declared). If instead some actual creature later becomes a blocking creature for the attacking creature (i.e., a creature is declared or otherwise caused to block), then the Retaliation-granted ability would trigger at the moment that creature becomes a blocking creature for the attacker (rule 509.3f).

Reasoning: To “cast” a spell means to take the card from where it is, put it on the stack, and pay its costs (see rule 601.2b). When a player plays an adventurer card, that player chooses whether to play the card normally (as the permanent spell) or as its Adventure (see rule 715.3d). Spell Queller’s leaves-the-battlefield ability allows Aydan to cast the exiled card without paying its mana cost as part of that ability’s resolution, and the player can’t wait to cast it later; importantly, timing permissions based on the card’s type are ignored for that cast (see [Spell Queller ruling #3]). Spell Queller’s rules also say the spell you cast from exile has no relation to the original spell that was exiled (see [Spell Queller ruling #2]). Kellan, the Fae-Blooded // Birthright Boon’s adventure-specific ruling that an adventurer card exiled by some other means won’t itself grant the adventure’s usual later permission to be cast as a permanent (see [Kellan, the Fae-Blooded // Birthright Boon ruling #4]) doesn’t stop Spell Queller from separately granting you permission to cast the card; it only says the card won’t independently be giving you the adventure’s after-resolution permission. Therefore, when resolving Spell Queller’s leaves-the-battlefield ability Aydan may choose whether to cast Birthright Boon (the Adventure sorcery half) or Kellan, the Fae-Blooded (the creature half).

results.question: Can Nicolas cast [Memory Lapse] targeting Aubrianna's [Underworld Charger] that is escaping from their graveyard?
results.text: Yes. Nicolas may cast Memory Lapse targeting Aubrianna's Underworld Charger while Aubrianna is casting Underworld Charger from her graveyard using its escape ability. Escape is a static ability that lets a player cast the card from their graveyard (702.138a); when Aubrianna casts Underworld Charger this way it becomes a spell on the stack as part of the casting process (601.2b). Memory Lapse’s text is “Counter target spell,” so Memory Lapse can target any spell on the stack, including a spell cast from a graveyard via escape (Memory Lapse). Underworld Charger’s rulings confirm that escape doesn’t change when the card may be cast from the graveyard and that an escaped card can be cast immediately if legal to do so (Underworld Charger ruling #0; Underworld Charger ruling #5). If Memory Lapse resolves and counters Aubrianna’s Underworld Charger, Memory Lapse’s replacement effect will put that spell on top of its owner’s library instead of into the graveyard (Memory Lapse ruling #0).

results.question: Ariyah has [Guardian Naga] in their graveyard. Can they flash back Guardian Naga's Adventure with [Flashback]?
results.text:
No. Ariyah cannot target Guardian Naga // Banishing Coils in their graveyard with Flashback to cast Banishing Coils while the card is in the graveyard.

Reasoning and definitions
- Flashback is a keyword that “means ‘You may cast this card from your graveyard if the resulting spell is an instant or sorcery spell by paying [cost] rather than paying its mana cost’ and ‘If the flashback cost was paid, exile this card instead of putting it anywhere else any time it would leave the stack.’” (See rule 702.34a and the Flashback card text.) The Flashback instant’s text is “Target instant or sorcery card in your graveyard gains flashback until end of turn.” That wording requires the targeted object in the graveyard to be an instant or sorcery card in the graveyard (Flashback card text).
- An Adventure card has alternative characteristics for an Adventure spell (the inset frame). Those alternative characteristics apply while the card is a spell (715.2a, 715.3a, 715.3b). If a card was cast as its Adventure, it is exiled as it resolves rather than put into the graveyard (715.3d and Guardian Naga // Banishing Coils ruling #2). An effect that refers to a card that “has an Adventure” may treat the card as having those alternative characteristics even when they’re not being used, but only if the effect explicitly refers to a card that “has an Adventure” (Guardian Naga // Banishing Coils ruling #7).

Because Guardian Naga // Banishing Coils sitting in the graveyard is the card’s normal characteristics (a creature card with an Adventure printed on it) and is not itself an instant or sorcery card in the graveyard, it is not a legal target for the Flashback instant (702.34a; 715.2a; Flashback card text). Flashback can target only a card that is already an instant or sorcery card in the graveyard; Flashback does not say “target a card that has an Adventure” and you have no rule here that makes Guardian Naga // Banishing Coils an instant card while in the graveyard. Therefore you can’t use Flashback to give Guardian Naga // Banishing Coils’s Banishing Coils Adventure flashback from the graveyard.

Assumption about timing: this answer assumes Guardian Naga // Banishing Coils is simply in the graveyard (it wasn’t exiled as the result of being cast as its Adventure). If an effect explicitly made Guardian Naga // Banishing Coils be treated as an instant or sorcery card in the graveyard, or an effect explicitly referred to the card “that has an Adventure,” the result could be different (see Guardian Naga // Banishing Coils ruling #7 and 715.3d).

results.question: Ace controls [Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker] and activates its ability, turning it into a creature. They then play a second Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker. What happens when the second Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker resolves?
results.text:
When the second Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker resolves and enters the battlefield, both Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker will be on the battlefield and Ace must choose one of the two Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker to keep; the other is put into its owner’s graveyard.

Why: The second Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker resolves as a permanent and enters the battlefield (see rule 608.3a). State-based actions are then checked automatically (see rule 704.1). The legend rule says that if a player controls two or more legendary permanents with the same name, that player chooses one to keep and the rest are put into their owners’ graveyards (see rule 704.5j). Because Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker is a legendary permanent (see Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker card data), Ace chooses which copy of Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker remains and the other is put into Ace’s graveyard.

Definitions: A state-based action is an automatic game action that happens whenever certain conditions are met and that doesn’t use the stack (rule 704.1). The “legend rule” is the state-based action that causes a player who controls two or more legendary permanents with the same name to choose one to keep and put the rest into their owners’ graveyards (rule 704.5j).

Assumption about timing: This assumes the timing described (second Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker finishes resolving and enters the battlefield, then SBAs are checked). If, for example, the second Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker somehow entered as a copy of the first Sarkhan, the same legend-rule choice still applies when both are on the battlefield (see Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker card data and ruling).

results.question: Ainsley controls [Reconnaissance] and attacks Nancy with [Loxodon Wayfarer]. After combat damage is dealt, can Ainsley use Reconnaissance's activated ability to untap Loxodon Wayfarer?
results.text:
Yes. Assuming you mean “after combat damage is dealt” but still before the end of combat step ends (i.e., the moment after combat damage has been assigned and dealt but while the combat damage step is still ongoing and before the end of combat step finishes), Ainsley may activate Reconnaissance’s {0} ability to remove Loxodon Wayfarer from combat and untap Loxodon Wayfarer, provided Ainsley has priority.

Reasoning and definitions:
- Reconnaissance’s activated ability is “{0}: Remove target attacking creature you control from combat and untap it.” Activating an activated ability requires the controller to have priority (see rules 117.1 and 117.1b), so Ainsley can activate the ability whenever Ainsley has priority. (Also note a player can’t activate an activated ability of an object outside their range of influence; see rule 801.6.)
- “Removed from combat” means a permanent is removed from combat if it leaves the battlefield, its controller changes, it phases out, an effect specifically removes it from combat, and so on; a creature removed from combat stops being an attacking creature (see rule 506.4b). Reconnaissance’s ability is an effect that specifically removes the target attacking creature you control from combat, so it performs that removal and untaps the creature.
- Because the combat damage has already been dealt, removing Loxodon Wayfarer from combat and untapping Loxodon Wayfarer will not undo the combat damage that has been dealt. Reconnaissance’s ruling also notes it does not undo any effects that triggered on declaration of attackers or blockers (Reconnaissance ruling #0).

Timing caveat: If by “after combat damage is dealt” you instead mean “after the end of combat step has finished and the postcombat main phase has begun,” then Ainsley cannot target Loxodon Wayfarer with Reconnaissance’s ability as an attacking creature because as soon as the end of combat step ends all creatures stop being attacking and are removed from combat (see rule 511.3). If Ainsley waits until the end of combat step itself to activate the ability, Reconnaissance’s parenthetical text means the creature will untap after it deals combat damage if activated during the end of combat step; since combat damage already occurred, that untap timing is consistent with the ability still untapping Loxodon Wayfarer.

Short summary: yes if Ainsley has priority before the end of combat step finishes; no if the game has already moved past the end of combat step and into the postcombat main phase.

results.question: Arjun controls [Thermopod] and has no cards in their graveyard. Assuming they have enough mana, can they activate [Molten-Tail Masticore]'s first activated ability?
results.text:
No. Arjun can’t activate Molten-Tail Masticore’s “{4}, Exile a creature card from your graveyard: This creature deals 4 damage to any target.” activated ability because Arjun has no creature card in their graveyard to exile as part of that ability’s cost.

Reasoning: An activated ability is written with a cost and an effect and is activated by paying its cost [602.1]. A player can’t pay a cost without having the necessary resources to pay it fully (for example, you can’t pay a cost that requires exiling a creature card from your graveyard if you control no creature card in your graveyard) [118.3]. Because Arjun can’t pay the “Exile a creature card from your graveyard” portion of Molten-Tail Masticore’s activation cost, they can’t begin to activate that ability [602.5]. Thermopod’s presence doesn’t change this requirement; the activation specifically requires exiling a creature card from Arjun’s graveyard, which Arjun cannot do with no cards there (Thermopod’s abilities do not provide a way to satisfy that exile-as-cost requirement).

results.question: Can Ashley pay {B}{B}{B}{B}{B}{B} to cast [Beseech the Queen] or is Ashley limited to only paying {B}{B}{B} to do so?
results.text: Ashley can pay {B}{B}{B}{B}{B}{B} to cast Beseech the Queen. Each {2/B} in Beseech the Queen’s cost is a hybrid symbol (a mana symbol that can be paid in multiple ways); when Ashley proposes casting Beseech the Queen she must announce the nonhybrid equivalent cost she intends to pay and may choose for each {2/B} to be paid as {2} (generic) or as {B} (black). If Ashley chooses all three {2/B} symbols to be the {2} option, the nonhybrid equivalent total cost is {6}, and Ashley may pay that {6} with six black mana ({B}{B}{B}{B}{B}{B}). The card’s official ruling gives those exact examples, including {6} as a valid nonhybrid equivalent for Beseech the Queen. Also note that once the total cost is determined it becomes locked in before payment.

results.question: Arielle has [Blessed Hippogriff] in their graveyard. Arielle casts [Mission Briefing], can they choose to cast the adventure of Blessed Hippogriff?
results.text:
No. Mission Briefing can’t choose to cast the Adventure Tyr's Blessing from Blessed Hippogriff // Tyr's Blessing while Blessed Hippogriff // Tyr's Blessing is in your graveyard.

Reasoning: An “adventurer card” is a card with a two‑part frame and alternative characteristics for its Adventure (see rule 715.1 and the definition of alternative characteristics in rule 715.2a). However, an adventurer card “in every zone except the stack” has only its normal characteristics (rule 715.4). Blessed Hippogriff // Tyr's Blessing’s normal characteristics are a creature (the Blessed Hippogriff creature half); its Adventure half Tyr's Blessing is only the card’s alternative characteristics that exist while it’s on the stack as an Adventure (rules 715.2a and 715.4). Mission Briefing instructs you to choose “an instant or sorcery card in your graveyard”; because Blessed Hippogriff // Tyr's Blessing in the graveyard has only its normal creature characteristics, it is not an instant or sorcery there and so is not a legal choice. The only provided exception for using an Adventure’s alternative characteristics while choosing is when an effect specifically instructs you to choose a card name (Blessed Hippogriff // Tyr's Blessing ruling #9), which is not what Mission Briefing does.

Assumption: I assume the timing and zones described in the question are as written (Blessed Hippogriff // Tyr's Blessing is in the graveyard when Mission Briefing resolves). If Blessed Hippogriff // Tyr's Blessing were exiled as an Adventure (exiled after being cast as Tyr's Blessing), different rules apply to casting from exile (see the Adventure exile rules), but that situation isn’t what was asked.

results.question: Neriah controls [Cliffhaven Sell-Sword]. Ari casts [Oubliette] targeting it. Will Cliffhaven Sell-Sword phase back in at the beginning of Neriah's next untap step?
results.text:
No. Cliffhaven Sell-Sword will not phase in at the beginning of Neriah’s next untap step; it remains phased out until Oubliette leaves the battlefield, at which point it phases in immediately (and per Oubliette’s text it is tapped as it phases in).  

Reasoning and definitions:  
- Phasing is a static ability that modifies the untap step: during a player’s untap step, all phased-in permanents with phasing that player controls phase out, and all phased-out permanents that had phased out under that player’s control phase in (this is the phasing turn-based action) [702.26a, 502.1].  
- Oubliette’s ability causes a creature to “phase out until this enchantment leaves the battlefield,” which is the kind of one-shot effect that creates an initial phase-out and a matching one-shot that will cause the permanent to phase in when the specified event (Oubliette leaving the battlefield) occurs [Oubliette; 610.4].  
- However, a permanent phased out “this way” (by an effect saying “until” some event) doesn’t phase in as a result of the normal untap-step phasing; it phases in only when the specified event occurs (and then the second one-shot effect is created immediately after that event) [610.4a]. Oubliette’s official ruling restates this interaction: a creature phased out by Oubliette doesn’t phase in during its controller’s untap step and instead phases in immediately after Oubliette leaves the battlefield [Oubliette ruling #7].  
- When the creature does phase in after Oubliette leaves, Oubliette’s text also instructs that the creature is tapped as it phases in (so Cliffhaven Sell-Sword will be tapped when it phases in) [Oubliette].  

Multiplayer note: This outcome is the same in multiplayer as long as Oubliette remains on the battlefield; special multiplayer rules about players leaving the game only matter if a player or their permanents leave the game (see rules about phased-out permanents when a player leaves) [702.26n, 800.4a].

results.question: Nico controls [Lazav, the Multifarious], which is currently a copy of [Lazav, Dimir Mastermind]. Abram discards [Kasimir the Lone Wolf] due to hand size at the end of their turn. Lazav, the Multifarious's ability triggers. After it resolves, what is Lazav, the Multifarious named?
results.text: After the ability resolves, Lazav, the Multifarious is named "Lazav, the Multifarious."  When Lazav, the Multifarious’s triggered ability resolves, Lazav, the Multifarious becomes a copy of Kasimir the Lone Wolf except its name is Lazav, the Multifarious (and it gains the other exceptions the ability lists). "Becomes a copy of" means the object acquires the copiable values of the chosen card (name, mana cost, color indicator, card type, subtype, supertype, rules text, power, toughness, and/or loyalty) as printed on that card, as modified by copy effects; copy effects can include modifications such as "except its name is ...," and those modifications become part of the copiable values. Therefore the result is an object with Kasimir the Lone Wolf’s printed copiable values but with its name set to Lazav, the Multifarious (Lazav, the Multifarious ruling #1 confirms Lazav copies exactly what was printed except for the characteristics it specifically modifies).

results.question: Alivia has [Road // Ruin] in their graveyard. Alivia casts [Torrential Gearhulk]. Which side of Road // Ruin can Alivia cast with its trigger?
results.text:
Alivia can cast Road (the instant half of Road // Ruin) with Torrential Gearhulk’s triggered ability; Alivia can’t cast Ruin (the sorcery half) with that trigger.

Why: While Road // Ruin is in the graveyard it has the combined characteristics of both halves, so it can be targeted as an instant card (Road // Ruin ruling #3). When you actually cast a split card you put only the half you’re casting onto the stack (Road // Ruin ruling #0). Torrential Gearhulk’s ability specifically lets you cast a target instant card from your graveyard, and the half you put on the stack must be an instant to satisfy that wording (Torrential Gearhulk ruling #0). Ruin is the sorcery half, so it would not be the instant half required by Torrential Gearhulk’s ability; Road is the instant half and so is the only half you may cast with that trigger.

Definitions/notes: “To cast” means to take the card from its zone, put it on the stack, and pay costs (rule 601.2b). A split card that’s not on the stack has the combination of both halves’ characteristics (Road // Ruin ruling #3), but when casting you choose which half to put on the stack and only that half’s characteristics are relevant (Road // Ruin ruling #0). Also, if you cast the card with Torrential Gearhulk’s ability, you cast it as part of that ability’s resolution (Torrential Gearhulk ruling #0).

results.question: Alvaro controls [Draugr Thought-Thief] and [Lotusguard Disciple]. Nico controls [Sands of Time] and [Yurlok of Scorch Thrash]. If Alvaro casts [Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats], can they choose to only have the cost reduced by {1}?
results.text: No. You can’t choose to apply only part of Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats’s cost reduction — the spell’s total cost is reduced by {1} for each creature in your party, and those cost reductions are applied when the total cost is determined and become locked in; you may not change the count after you begin to cast the spell. (Whether Draugr Thought-Thief and Lotusguard Disciple both count as creatures in Alvaro’s party isn’t defined in the provided rules, so I can’t say whether the reduction would be {1} or {2} in this specific board state.)

results.question: Adriel controls [Oko, Thief of Crowns], [Gilded Goose], and a Food token. Adriel uses Oko, Thief of Crowns's +1 ability to make the Food token into a 3/3 Elk. Can Adriel then sacrifice it to Gilded Goose?
results.text:
No. While Oko, Thief of Crowns's +1 ability has made the Food token a 3/3 green Elk, you can't sacrifice that permanent to Gilded Goose's “{T}, Sacrifice a Food: Add one mana of any color” ability because it is no longer a Food artifact.

Reasoning: The object began as a Food token, which is a colorless Food artifact token (Food token and [111.10b]). A token can be affected by effects that change card types ([111.6]). Oko, Thief of Crowns's +1 ability makes the target “a green Elk creature” and, as explained in Oko, Thief of Crowns ruling #5, the effect causes the object to lose other card types it has (such as artifact), leaving it just a green Elk creature. Gilded Goose's ability requires sacrificing “a Food,” and Gilded Goose ruling #0 defines “a Food” to mean “any Food artifact.” Because the Food token targeted by Oko, Thief of Crowns is no longer an artifact while that continuous effect applies, it does not qualify as “a Food” and therefore cannot be sacrificed to pay Gilded Goose's cost. (To sacrifice means to move a permanent you control from the battlefield to its owner's graveyard; see [701.21a].)

If Oko, Thief of Crowns's effect ends and the permanent becomes a Food artifact again, you may then sacrifice that Food artifact to pay Gilded Goose's cost.

results.question: Natasha controls a [Lifeline] and 2 [Scarwood Goblins]. Adriel casts [Plague Wind]. Does Lifeline trigger and return the creatures to the battlefield at the beginning of the next end step?
results.text:
Lifeline will trigger twice when the two Scarwood Goblins die, but in the situation described none of the Scarwood Goblins will be returned at the beginning of the next end step because Lifeline’s intervening‑if condition won’t be true when those delayed abilities resolve.

Definition: “Dies” means “is put into a graveyard from the battlefield.” [700.4]

Reasoning: Plague Wind destroys Natasha’s two Scarwood Goblins, so each Scarwood Goblins dying is a separate occurrence and causes Lifeline to trigger once for each dead creature. [603.2c] Lifeline’s triggered ability contains an intervening‑if clause (“if another creature is on the battlefield”), and Lifeline’s ruling explains that if all creatures on the battlefield go to the graveyard at once, none of them are returned because the intervening‑if is not true when the delayed abilities would resolve. [Lifeline ruling #0] In the given position Natasha only had the two Scarwood Goblins as creatures, both die simultaneously and no creatures remain on the battlefield, so at the beginning of the next end step the condition is false and the delayed triggers do nothing. If there were a creature on the battlefield when each delayed ability resolves, each Scarwood Goblins would be returned one at a time. [Lifeline ruling #4]

results.question: Alfred casts [Stream of Thought], replicating it twice. Nico controls [Chalice of the Void] with 1 charge counter. What happens?
results.text:
Alfred’s two replicate copies of Stream of Thought are created and resolve first; after those copies resolve, Chalice of the Void’s triggered ability will counter the original Stream of Thought (the original spell itself does not resolve).

Why: Replicate means “When you cast this spell, if a replicate cost was paid for it, copy it for each time its replicate cost was paid” and Alfred paid Stream of Thought’s replicate cost twice, so two copies are created when Stream of Thought was cast [702.56a]. The copy effect created by replicate puts copies of Stream of Thought onto the stack; a copy of a spell is not cast (it’s put onto the stack by the copy effect) [707.10]. Chalice of the Void’s ability triggers only when a player casts a spell with mana value equal to its charge counters, so it triggered when Alfred cast Stream of Thought (Stream of Thought’s mana value is 1), and that triggered ability can counter the original Stream of Thought when that trigger resolves (Chalice of the Void’s text).

Stream of Thought’s replicate-related rulings make the interaction clear: you get a copy for each time you paid the replicate cost even if the original spell is later countered [Stream of Thought ruling #3], and if you replicate Stream of Thought the copies resolve before the original spell, so those copies can’t shuffle the original Stream of Thought into your library while the original is still on the stack [Stream of Thought ruling #1]. Practically, the two copies each resolve (each copy mills the chosen target player for four and then allows Alfred to shuffle up to four cards from Alfred’s graveyard into Alfred’s library, though not the original Stream of Thought because it’s still on the stack), and later the Chalice of the Void triggered ability resolves and counters the original Stream of Thought, so the original does nothing further.

Assumption about timing: this answer assumes the normal ordering where triggered abilities created by casting Stream of Thought (the replicate copy-creating trigger) and Chalet of the Void’s triggered ability are placed on the stack and then resolve; the rulings cited determine that the replicate copies resolve before the original regardless of the original being countered [Stream of Thought ruling #1, Stream of Thought ruling #3]. If an alternative trigger-ordering detail were specified, the end result (copies still resolve; the original is countered) is unchanged because of those rulings.

results.question: Adrienne attacks with [Sporeweb Weaver], and Nicolas blocks it with [Serpent Assassin]. Can Nicolas use [Tishana's Tidebinder] to counter Sporeweb Weaver's ability?
results.text:
I can’t answer definitively with only the provided rules. The context tells us when Sporeweb Weaver’s ability triggers (damage is dealt) and that you can’t cast spells during the damage-assignment/ dealing action, but the provided rules don’t say whether a player can cast Tishana's Tidebinder in a window that would let its enter-the-battlefield triggered ability target and counter Sporeweb Weaver’s triggered ability before that triggered ability is put onto the stack.

Definitions and what the given rules do establish
- Triggered ability: a triggered ability is written “[When/Whenever/At] [trigger condition or event], [effect]. [Instructions (if any).]” (603.1). Sporeweb Weaver’s ability is a triggered ability that triggers “Whenever this creature is dealt damage.”
- When the damage event occurs: damage is dealt as part of the combat damage step; no player may cast spells or activate abilities between the time combat damage is assigned and the time it’s dealt (510.2). When damage is dealt, abilities that trigger when damage is dealt “trigger now and wait to be put on the stack” (120.4b). Sporeweb Weaver’s ability will trigger even if the damage causes Sporeweb Weaver to die ([Sporeweb Weaver ruling #2]).
- Tishana's Tidebinder’s relevant text: “When this creature enters, counter up to one target activated or triggered ability.” To have that effect counter Sporeweb Weaver’s triggered ability, Tishana's Tidebinder must enter the battlefield and its enter-the-battlefield triggered ability must be able to target the Sporeweb Weaver triggered ability.

What is missing from the provided rules (why I can’t answer)
- The provided rules do not state exactly when triggered abilities are put onto the stack relative to the next moments players get priority after damage is dealt, or whether there is any window after damage is dealt in which a player may cast spells before those damage-triggered abilities are placed on the stack. (120.4b says they “wait to be put on the stack,” but does not say whether players get priority before that happens or only after they are actually on the stack.)
- The provided rules do not say whether an ability that is in the state “waiting to be put on the stack” can be targeted by spells or abilities (necessary for Tishana's Tidebinder’s enter-the-battlefield triggered ability to target it) before it is actually on the stack.

Because those specific timing/targeting details are not included in the supplied rules and card data, I must set answered = false rather than guess.

Assumption note: if you were assuming a timing where Tishana's Tidebinder is already on the battlefield before combat damage is dealt, then its enter-the-battlefield triggered ability is already resolved and cannot be used then; the question as asked implies Nicolas would cast Tishana's Tidebinder in response to the damage-trigger, which is precisely the timing detail the provided rules leave ambiguous.

results.question: Autumn controls [Captain Mar-Vell, Space-Born] and casts [Tempted by the Oriq] targeting Breanna's and Case's Soldier tokens. Before it resolves, Autumn casts [Insurrection]. What happens?
results.text:
Direct answer: Insurrection resolves first (it was cast in response), so Autumn gains control of all creatures until end of turn (that includes Breanna’s Soldier token and Case’s Soldier token). After Insurrection resolves, Tempted by the Oriq checks its targets and finds that the chosen creatures are no longer creatures “that [Breanna/Case] control,” so Tempted by the Oriq has no legal targets for those instances and therefore doesn’t resolve; put Tempted by the Oriq into Autumn’s graveyard and no control-change from that spell happens.

Why: “In response to” means a spell cast while another is on the stack goes on top and will resolve first (117.7, 405.2). When the players let the stack resolve, the topmost object resolves first (608.1, 405.5). Insurrection’s text is “Untap all creatures and gain control of them until end of turn. They gain haste until end of turn,” so when Insurrection resolves Autumn gains control of all creatures, including the two Soldier tokens (Insurrection card data). When Tempted by the Oriq tries to resolve, the game checks whether its targets are still legal. A target that is no longer controlled by the player referenced by the spell is an illegal target; if all targets for every instance of the word “target” are illegal, the spell doesn’t resolve and, if it’s a spell, it’s put into its owner’s graveyard (608.2b). Because Autumn now controls those tokens, they are no longer legal targets for the parts of Tempted by the Oriq that say “target creature or planeswalker that player controls with mana value 3 or less,” so Tempted by the Oriq doesn’t resolve (Tempted by the Oriq card data, 608.2b).

Assumption/Timing note: This assumes the sequence you described (Autumn casts Tempted by the Oriq, then while it’s on the stack Autumn casts Insurrection “in response” to it). If instead Insurrection had resolved earlier (before Tempted by the Oriq was cast), the same end result applies at resolution time because target legality is always checked when Tempted by the Oriq resolves (608.2b).

results.question: Amelia casts [Aminatou's Augury] exiling an artifact and an instant. Afterwards Amelia casts another Aminatou's Augury, which exiles an instant. Can they cast both instants?
results.text:
Yes. Amelia may cast both instants: the instant exiled by the first Aminatou's Augury and the instant exiled by the second Aminatou's Augury, each under the permission created by the Aminatou's Augury that exiled it. 

Definition (linked abilities): A “linked” pair of abilities is when an object’s printed ability exiles one or more cards and another printed ability on the same object refers to the exiled cards; the second ability refers only to the cards exiled by that object [607.2a].

Why: Each resolution of Aminatou's Augury exiles its own set of cards and creates the permission that lets you cast spells of those nonland types from among the cards it exiled until end of turn. Because those abilities are linked to the specific Aminatou's Augury that exiled those cards, the first Aminatou's Augury’s permission applies to the instant it exiled and the second Aminatou's Augury’s permission applies to the instant it exiled [607.2a]. Casting one of those exiled instants causes that card to leave exile when you cast it, and you can’t cast that same exiled card multiple times [Aminatou's Augury ruling #6]; that doesn’t stop you from also casting the other instant that was exiled by the other Aminatou's Augury. To actually cast those instants you must have priority and follow the normal casting process (moving the card from exile to the stack and paying any costs — here the Augury permissions waive the mana cost) [117.1a; 601.2a; 601.3f].

Yes. After Acrobatic Maneuver resolves and returns Gisa and Geralf to the battlefield, Aubrey may cast another Zombie creature spell from their graveyard that turn.

Reasoning: Gisa and Geralf’s ability is “Once during each of your turns, you may cast a Zombie creature spell from your graveyard” (Gisa and Geralf). Acrobatic Maneuver’s text is “Exile target creature you control, then return that card to the battlefield under its owner's control” (Acrobatic Maneuver). If you cast one Zombie creature spell from your graveyard and then have a new Gisa and Geralf come under your control in the same turn, you may cast another Zombie creature spell from your graveyard that turn ([Gisa and Geralf ruling #3]). Exiling and then returning Gisa and Geralf causes that card to leave and re-enter the battlefield, which is the situation covered by “[a] new Gisa and Geralf come under your control” in that ruling, so the ability can be used again that turn. Note that a player can begin to cast a spell only if a rule or effect allows that player to cast it (601.3e), and Gisa and Geralf’s permission is what allows the extra cast.

Assumption about timing: I assume Aubrey already used Gisa and Geralf’s once-per-turn permission earlier that turn before Acrobatic Maneuver resolved. If Aubrey hadn’t already used it earlier, they would just have their one normal use after Gisa and Geralf is on the battlefield; the ruling above matters only when a second use is in question.

Additional note: Once you begin to cast the Zombie spell, losing control of Gisa and Geralf won’t affect that spell ([Gisa and Geralf ruling #2]).

results.question: In a game of commander, Natasha has shuffled their commander into their library. Adan casts [Praetor's Grasp] targeting Natasha and finds Natasha's commander. Can Natasha choose to put it into the command zone?
results.text:
Yes. When Praetor's Grasp exiles Natasha’s commander from Natasha’s library, Natasha may choose to put that card into the command zone as a state-based action when state-based actions are next checked, instead of leaving it in exile.

Reasoning and rules applied:
- A commander remains a commander in all zones (so the card Praetor's Grasp finds is still Natasha’s commander) [903.3e].
- Praetor's Grasp exiles the chosen card from Natasha’s library; that causes Natasha’s commander to be put into exile. Because the card was put into exile since the last time state-based actions were checked, Natasha may put Natasha’s commander into the command zone as a state-based action [903.9a]; the special Commander state-based-action rule describing this is explicitly stated in the Commander rules [704.6d].
- The replacement option in rule 903.9b (which lets an owner put a commander into the command zone instead of it being put into that owner’s hand or library) does not apply here, because Natasha’s commander is being put into exile, not into Natasha’s hand or library [903.9b].
- If Natasha elects not to move Natasha’s commander to the command zone and it remains exiled, Praetor's Grasp’s normal permission to let an opponent play the exiled card still applies (playing it must follow the normal rules for playing that card) [Praetor's Grasp ruling #1].

Timing assumption: I assume the sequence is that Praetor's Grasp searches Natasha’s library and exiles Natasha’s commander during resolution, and then state-based actions are checked immediately afterward. If Natasha’s commander had already been in exile from before state-based actions were last checked, the trigger in 903.9a/704.6d would not apply until it is newly put into exile.

results.question: Nico controls [Lion's Eye Diamond]. Addison casts [Wipe Away] targeting the Lion's Eye Diamond. Can Nico activate it in response?

Activate only as an instant.” ability is a mana ability is the point you must know to resolve this interaction.

- “In response to”: A spell or activated ability cast or activated while another spell or ability is already on the stack is cast or activated “in response to” the earlier one (rule 117.7).

What’s missing and why it matters: rule 605.1’s criteria that list which activated abilities are mana abilities are not present in the provided excerpt. That rule is the necessary piece to determine whether Lion's Eye Diamond’s ability counts as a mana ability despite having non-mana costs (discard your hand and sacrifice this artifact). Without that text, the correct ruling cannot be deduced from the supplied material.

Assumption/alternate timing note: I assume standard timing where Addison casts Wipe Away targeting Lion's Eye Diamond and the spell is on the stack; the question asks whether Nico can activate Lion's Eye Diamond in response. If Lion's Eye Diamond is a mana ability under the missing criteria, the activation is allowed; if not, it is disallowed.
