results.question: Alex controls [Rhythm of the Wild], [Grumgully, the Generous], [Renata, Called to the Hunt], and [Hardened Scales]. Alex then casts [Grizzled Outrider]. If they chooses to put a counter on Grizzled Outrider for Rhythm of the Wild, how many +1/+1 counters will it enter with in total?
results.text:
Grizzled Outrider will enter the battlefield with four +1/+1 counters on it.

Reasoning: Rhythm of the Wild gives your nontoken creature Riot, meaning Grizzled Outrider can enter with your choice of a +1/+1 counter (you chose that option) (Rhythm of the Wild). Grumgully, the Generous’s ability causes each other non-Human creature you control to enter with an additional +1/+1 counter (Grumgully, the Generous). Renata, Called to the Hunt’s ability causes each other creature you control to enter with an additional +1/+1 counter (Renata, Called to the Hunt). Those three effects would put a total of three +1/+1 counters on Grizzled Outrider as it enters. Hardened Scales then modifies that event: “If a creature you control would enter the battlefield with a number of +1/+1 counters on it, it enters with that many plus one instead,” so Grizzled Outrider enters with 3 + 1 = 4 +1/+1 counters (Hardened Scales; [Hardened Scales ruling #0]).

results.question: Ann has a [Sphere of Resistance], a Plains and a Swamp. Can Ann cast [Prismatic Ending] targeting [Drake Familiar]?
results.text:
Yes. Ann can cast Prismatic Ending targeting Drake Familiar by choosing X = 0 and paying the total cost {1}{W} (the extra {1} comes from Sphere of Resistance) using Plains for {W} and Swamp for the {1}, thereby spending two colors of mana (W and B) so Prismatic Ending’s Converge can exile Drake Familiar (mana value 2).

Reasoning and assumptions:
- Prismatic Ending is a sorcery that exiles a target nonland permanent (so it requires you to choose a permanent as a target when casting) and Drake Familiar is a creature permanent on the battlefield, so it is a legal target when you choose targets as part of casting the spell [601.2c], [115.2].
- A player may begin to cast a spell only if allowed and not prohibited; nothing in the position given prevents Ann from beginning to cast Prismatic Ending, so she may proceed [601.3].
- Sphere of Resistance’s text makes spells cost {1} more to cast (Sphere of Resistance). That increases the generic portion of Prismatic Ending’s cost, so the total cost to cast Prismatic Ending becomes {X+1}{W} (developer guidance: show the cost by symbol). For X = 0 that is {1}{W} (Sphere of Resistance plus the printed {W}).
- Ann can pay {W} with Plains and the generic {1} with Swamp’s {B} (generic mana can be paid with colored mana). The colors of mana actually spent to cast the spell are W and B (two colors). Prismatic Ending’s Converge cares about the number of colors of mana spent to cast it; per the card’s ruling, the spell can exile a nonland permanent whose mana value is less than or equal to the number of colors of mana spent to cast the spell (Prismatic Ending ruling #0). Drake Familiar’s mana value is 2, so spending two colors (W and B) meets that requirement.

I assumed Drake Familiar is on the battlefield and both Plains and Swamp can produce their respective mana (i.e., they are untapped and able to be tapped for mana). If Ann couldn’t actually produce those two mana (for example, one land was already tapped or an effect prevented producing mana), she might not be able to cast it in this way.

results.question: Abram attacks with [Robber of the Rich], exiling [Skewer the Critics] from Nico's library. Can Abram pay Skewer the Critics's Spectacle cost with only {C}?
results.text: Yes. Abram can pay Skewer the Critics’s spectacle cost using only {C}, provided an opponent lost life this turn and Abram is casting the card at a time he’s allowed to cast that sorcery (for example, during his main phase when the stack is empty). Reasoning: Spectacle is an alternative cost that lets you pay the spectacle cost instead of the spell’s mana cost if the spectacle condition is met [702.137a]. When you cast Skewer the Critics you choose whether to pay its spectacle cost and determine the total cost before paying anything [601.2b, 601.2f]. Skewer the Critics’s spectacle cost is {R} (the card’s printed text gives that alternative cost) [Skewer the Critics]. Robber of the Rich’s granted ability says you may “spend mana as though it were mana of any color to cast that spell,” which applies when you cast the exiled Skewer the Critics and affects how you may spend your mana as you pay costs for that casting [Robber of the Rich]. Because that ability changes how you may spend your mana while paying the spell’s costs, you may spend colorless mana ({C}) and treat it as red to pay the {R} spectacle cost when you actually pay costs. Note also that Skewer the Critics is a sorcery, and Robber of the Rich’s exile-based permission doesn’t change timing rules for the exiled card; you can cast the exiled Skewer the Critics only at times you could cast that sorcery (see Robber of the Rich ruling #7 and Skewer the Critics ruling #2) [Robber of the Rich ruling #7, Skewer the Critics ruling #2]. Assumption: an opponent lost life this turn (the spectacle condition); if that hasn’t happened, you can’t cast Skewer the Critics for its spectacle cost [702.137a].

results.question: Aspen controls [Haakon, Stromgald Scourge] and has [Foulmire Knight] in their graveyard. Can Aspen cast the Adventure portion of Foulmire Knight from their graveyard?
results.text:
No. Aspen cannot cast the Adventure Profane Insight of Foulmire Knight // Profane Insight from their graveyard while Haakon, Stromgald Scourge is providing its graveyard-casting ability; Haakon, Stromgald Scourge only lets you cast creature spells from your graveyard, and Profane Insight is the Adventure (an instant), not the creature half.

Definitions and short reasoning:
- An adventurer card is a card that has an Adventure; while it’s in a zone like the graveyard it has only its normal characteristics (so Foulmire Knight // Profane Insight is a creature card in the graveyard) and if you choose to cast it “as an Adventure” you use only the Adventure’s (alternative) characteristics while it’s on the stack (715.3a; 715.4; 715.2a). [Definitions]
- Haakon, Stromgald Scourge’s ability lets you cast Knight creature spells from your graveyard; casting such a card from the graveyard follows the normal rules for casting a creature spell (Haakon, Stromgald Scourge ruling #1). That ability does not say you may cast instants or Adventure spells from your graveyard, only creature spells. (601.3e’s examples show that an effect that allows casting spells of a particular type from another zone permits only that type — e.g., Garruk allows creature halves, Melek allows instant/sorcery halves.)
- The Adventure Profane Insight of Foulmire Knight // Profane Insight is an instant Adventure; to cast the Adventure you must cast the card as an Adventure and use the Adventure’s (instant) characteristics to determine legality (Foulmire Knight // Profane Insight ruling #2). Because Haakon, Stromgald Scourge allows casting creature spells from the graveyard, it doesn’t permit casting the Adventure Profane Insight (an instant) from the graveyard. (Foulmire Knight // Profane Insight is a creature card in the graveyard under normal characteristics, per Foulmire Knight // Profane Insight ruling #0; 715.4.)

Practical outcome: Aspen may cast the creature half Foulmire Knight // Profane Insight (the Foulmire Knight creature spell) from the graveyard while Haakon, Stromgald Scourge is on the battlefield, but Aspen may not cast the Adventure Profane Insight of Foulmire Knight // Profane Insight from the graveyard using Haakon, Stromgald Scourge’s ability.

Assumption: I assume the question concerns only Haakon, Stromgald Scourge’s graveyard-casting ability and not some other effect that separately allows casting instants or Adventures from the graveyard; if an effect explicitly allowed instants from the graveyard, the answer could change (601.3e; Foulmire Knight // Profane Insight ruling #2).

results.question: Ayaan controls [Essence of the Wild] and casts [Evil Twin]. Can they have the Evil Twin enter the battlefield as a copy of Nico's [Quakestrider Ceratops]?
results.text:
No. Evil Twin will enter the battlefield as a copy of Essence of the Wild, not as a copy of Nico's Quakestrider Ceratops.

Reasoning: A "replacement effect" is an effect that modifies how an event affects an object (for example, causing a permanent to enter the battlefield as a copy of something). When a permanent is entering the battlefield "as a copy," it becomes that copy as it enters the battlefield (it doesn’t enter and then become a copy) [707.5]. Evil Twin has a replacement option that may have it enter as a copy of a creature, and Essence of the Wild causes creatures you control to enter as a copy of Essence of the Wild; those are two replacement effects that would cause the same entering object to become a copy, so rule 616.1c applies. The official ruling for Essence of the Wild states that if a creature such as Clone (i.e., any creature with its own copy effect) is entering under your control while you control Essence of the Wild, there will be two copy effects to apply and “no matter what order these effects are applied, the creature will be a copy of Essence of the Wild when it enters” [Essence of the Wild ruling #6]. Applying that ruling here means Evil Twin will enter as a copy of Essence of the Wild rather than as a copy of Nico's Quakestrider Ceratops.

Assumption and alternate timing: This answer assumes Nico's Quakestrider Ceratops is already on the battlefield when Ayaan casts Evil Twin. If Evil Twin were entering the battlefield at the same time as another creature, Evil Twin can't become a copy of a creature that is entering at the same time [Evil Twin ruling #6].

results.question: Alex controls [Obosh, the Preypiercer] and casts their last card, [Flame Spill], targeting a 1/1 creature that Nevaeh controls. How much damage will Nevaeh take?
results.text:
Nevaeh will be dealt 6 damage.

Reasoning:
- Define “excess damage”: Excess damage is damage dealt to a creature greater than what would be lethal damage (damage in excess of that creature’s toughness after accounting for damage already marked on it); see Excess Damage and rule 120.4a. Flame Spill’s rules tell you to start with the amount being dealt to the creature and determine what is “lethal” (the creature’s toughness minus damage already marked on it, ignoring replacement or prevention effects) and then compute excess (Flame Spill ruling #0).
- Apply those steps to this situation: Flame Spill is attempting to deal 4 damage to Nevaeh’s 1/1 creature. Lethal damage to that 1/1 is 1, so the unmodified split is 1 damage to the creature and 3 excess damage to the creature’s controller (Nevaeh) (Flame Spill ruling #0 and Flame Spill ruling #1).
- Obosh, the Preypiercer’s effect doubles damage that an odd–mana-value source you control would deal to a permanent or player. Flame Spill has a mana value of 3 (odd), so Flame Spill is such a source; its damage is doubled (Obosh, the Preypiercer). Per Obosh, the unmodified assignment is done first and then the assigned amounts are doubled (Obosh, the Preypiercer ruling #6). Therefore the 1 assigned to the creature is doubled to 2, and the 3 excess assigned to Nevaeh is doubled to 6.
- The result is that Nevaeh is dealt 6 damage (Flame Spill ruling #1); that damage causes Nevaeh to lose that much life (rule 119.2).

Assumption: I assumed there were no other replacement or prevention effects affecting the damage. If a prevention or replacement effect applied before damage is dealt, it could change the final amounts (Flame Spill ruling #0 notes you ignore replacement/prevention when determining what is lethal, but actual damage can then be modified by replacement/prevention when it is dealt).

results.question: Alessandro activates [Inkmoth Nexus] to turn it into a creature and attacks Noor with it. Noor doesn't block it and then casts [Through the Breach], putting [Melira, Sylvok Outcast] onto the battlefield. What happens during the combat damage step?
results.text:
Direct answer: Assuming Through the Breach resolved and Melira, Sylvok Outcast entered the battlefield before combat damage is dealt, Inkmoth Nexus deals 1 regular point of combat damage to Noor (no poison counter and no -1/-1 counters are created). Melira, Sylvok Outcast’s continuous effect makes creatures your opponents control lose infect, so Inkmoth Nexus no longer has infect while Melira, Sylvok Outcast is on the battlefield; therefore the damage is normal damage equal to Inkmoth Nexus’s power (1). That damage is dealt in the combat damage step and processed as loss of life for Noor (not as poison counters). 

Reasoning and assumptions: 
- Definition: By the Inkmoth Nexus card text, infect causes a creature’s damage to players to be dealt in the form of poison counters and to creatures in the form of -1/-1 counters; Inkmoth Nexus becomes a 1/1 Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact creature with flying and infect while its ability is active. (Inkmoth Nexus) 
- I assume Through the Breach finished resolving and Melira, Sylvok Outcast is on the battlefield before combat damage is dealt. If Through the Breach instead resolved after combat damage was dealt, Melira, Sylvok Outcast would not affect that already-dealt damage. Note that after combat damage has been assigned, no player gets priority to cast spells before that damage is dealt (see rule [510.2]), so a player cannot cast Through the Breach in the window between assignment and the actual dealing of the damage. 
- As a result of Melira, Sylvok Outcast’s printed ability “Creatures your opponents control lose infect,” Inkmoth Nexus does not have infect while Melira, Sylvok Outcast is on the battlefield, so Inkmoth Nexus’s damage to Noor is not infection damage. (Melira, Sylvok Outcast) 
- During the combat damage step, each attacking creature deals combat damage equal to its power (Inkmoth Nexus is a 1/1 while it’s a creature), and all combat damage is dealt simultaneously as a turn-based action; that damage is then processed into results (life loss, counters, etc.). (120.2a; 510.2; 120.4b; 120.4c) 
- Because Melira, Sylvok Outcast also says “You can’t get poison counters,” Noor would in any case not receive poison counters while Melira, Sylvok Outcast is on the battlefield; and because Melira, Sylvok Outcast makes Inkmoth Nexus lose infect, no -1/-1 counters are involved either. (Melira, Sylvok Outcast) 

If you want the alternate timing: if Through the Breach did not resolve until after combat damage was dealt, then Inkmoth Nexus would deal its damage with whatever abilities it had at damage-dealing time (including infect, if Melira, Sylvok Outcast was not yet on the battlefield).

results.question: Alex controls [Extus, Oriq Overlord] and uses [Illithid Harvester] to try to turn it face down. What happens?
results.text:
Nothing happens — Illithid Harvester's triggered ability can’t turn Extus, Oriq Overlord face down, so Extus, Oriq Overlord stays face up with its printed characteristics unchanged. Reason: Illithid Harvester's triggered ability can’t target or turn double-faced cards face down (Illithid Harvester // Plant Tadpoles ruling #2), and double-faced permanents can’t be turned face down (rule [712.16]).

Definition: “Turn face down” means to change a face-up permanent so it becomes a face-down permanent; a double-faced permanent is a permanent represented by a double-faced card and, per [712.16], can’t be turned face down.

Assumption: I’m assuming Extus, Oriq Overlord is currently on the battlefield as the face-up double-faced permanent it normally is. If Extus, Oriq Overlord were not a double-faced permanent for some reason (for example, it were a token or copy not represented by a double-faced card), the cited ruling and rule wouldn’t apply and the result could be different.

results.question: Ayla controls [Living Plane] and plays [Minas Tirith]. Does it enter tapped or untapped?
results.text: Minas Tirith enters the battlefield tapped (unless Ayla already controls a legendary creature, in which case it would enter untapped). Living Plane doesn’t stop Minas Tirith’s “enters tapped” replacement effect from applying: Minas Tirith’s “enters tapped” is a replacement effect that modifies how it enters the battlefield [614.1c], and Living Plane is a continuous effect that makes lands into creatures once they are on the battlefield [Living Plane; 603.6b]. Minas Tirith’s untap condition requires that a legendary creature already be on the battlefield as the land enters; if no such legendary creature is already present, the land enters tapped [Minas Tirith ruling #0; 614.12]. (“Enters tapped” describes the permanent’s tapped status value as it enters the battlefield [110.5b].)

results.question: Andy controls [Badlands] and [Conversion]. Andy then casts [Magus of the Moon]. After that resolves, what color(s) of mana can Badlands tap for?
results.text:
Badlands can be tapped to produce either white mana ({W}) or red mana ({R}).

Reasoning and definitions:
- A mana ability is an ability that produces mana (see 605.1). Such abilities are relevant here because both the Plains intrinsic ability and the Magus-granted ability are {T}: Add ... mana abilities. (605.1)
- When Magus of the Moon’s continuous effect applies, nonbasic lands become Mountains and gain the ability “{T}: Add {R}.” (Magus of the Moon ruling #2)
- Conversion’s continuous effect makes all Mountains become Plains; there is no time window in which a land newly made a Mountain can be tapped for red before Conversion makes it a Plains. (Conversion ruling #1)
- When a land’s subtype is set to a basic land type, the land loses its old land type(s) and the abilities generated by those old land types and gains the appropriate mana ability for the new basic land type; Plains gives the intrinsic ability “{T}: Add {W}.” (305.7, 305.6)
- That process does not remove abilities that were granted to the land by other effects, so the ability Magus of the Moon granted (“{T}: Add {R}”) remains. (305.7; Magus of the Moon ruling #2)
- Putting this together: after Magus of the Moon resolves with Conversion already in play, Badlands ends up with the Plains intrinsic ability ({T}: Add {W}) because Mountains are turned into Plains by Conversion, and it also keeps the ability granted by Magus of the Moon ({T}: Add {R}). (Conversion ruling #1; 305.7; Magus of the Moon ruling #2)

Therefore Badlands can tap for either {W} or {R}.

Assumption/ordering note: I’ve assumed Conversion is already in effect when Magus of the Moon’s continuous effect is applied; Conversion ruling #1 addresses that timing by saying you don’t get to tap the just-created Mountain for red before it becomes a Plains. If Conversion weren’t in effect, Badlands would be a Mountain with Magus’s granted {T}: Add {R} (Magus of the Moon ruling #2).

results.question: Nico controls [Blind Obedience]. Adonis's devotion to black is 0 and they cast [Erebos, God of the Dead]. Does it enter the battlefield tapped or untapped?
results.text:
Erebos, God of the Dead enters the battlefield untapped.

Reasoning and definitions: Devotion to a color is the number of mana symbols of that color among the mana costs of permanents a player controls (definition: devotion to a color) [700.5a]. A replacement effect is a continuous effect that watches for an event and replaces it (definition: replacement effect) [614.1c]. Some static abilities that say things like “Permanents enter tapped” modify how permanents enter and function as replacement effects while the permanent is entering the battlefield [614.12]. Blind Obedience’s ability (“Artifacts and creatures your opponents control enter tapped”) is such a replacement-ish static effect that only applies to artifacts and creatures entering under an opponent’s control (see the Orb of Dreams example in [614.12] for a similar “Permanents enter tapped” effect).

[Erebos, God of the Dead ruling #6] says that as a God enters the battlefield, your devotion to its color (calculated before counting the God’s own mana symbols) determines whether replacement effects that affect creatures entering the battlefield apply to that God. Because Adonis’s devotion to black is 0 (and the God’s own {B} isn’t counted for that determination), Erebos, God of the Dead is not a creature as it is entering the battlefield. Therefore the part of Blind Obedience that makes creatures your opponents control enter tapped does not apply to Erebos, God of the Dead as it enters. Blind Obedience’s artifact clause doesn’t apply either because Erebos, God of the Dead is not an artifact. Nothing makes Erebos, God of the Dead enter tapped, so Erebos, God of the Dead enters the battlefield untapped. (Erebos, God of the Dead’s own type-changing/“isn't a creature” effect functions as it is entering the battlefield [113.6h], consistent with the ruling.)

This conclusion does not depend on the number of players at the table; the same interaction applies in multiplayer.

If you assumed a different timing (for example, if devotion were recalculated after Erebos, God of the Dead were already on the battlefield), the result would differ, but the provided ruling explicitly directs the devotion check to happen for the purpose of replacement effects as Erebos, God of the Dead is entering [Erebos, God of the Dead ruling #6].

results.question: Alex casts [Brainstorm] using the ability of [Jace, Telepath Unbound]. Nina casts [Memory Lapse] and counters Brainstorm. Where does Brainstorm go?
results.text:
Brainstorm is put on top of its owner’s library.

Reasoning: Alex cast Brainstorm from their graveyard using Jace, Vryn's Prodigy // Jace, Telepath Unbound’s −3 ability (that ability lets you cast the card from your graveyard and says “If that spell would be put into your graveyard, exile it instead”). Nina’s Memory Lapse counters Brainstorm and has the replacement effect “If that spell is countered this way, put it on top of its owner's library instead of into that player's graveyard.” Memory Lapse’s ruling explicitly states that Memory Lapse’s self-replacement effect replaces the spell going to the graveyard before any other effect can replace that event, so Memory Lapse’s replacement applies instead of Jace, Vryn's Prodigy // Jace, Telepath Unbound’s replacement-to-exile effect. Therefore Brainstorm is put on top of its owner’s library.

Definition: A replacement effect is an effect that modifies how an event would happen by replacing some or all of that event with a different event; here, two replacement effects would modify where Brainstorm goes after being countered, and Memory Lapse’s replacement takes precedence per its ruling.

Assumption: I’m assuming Brainstorm was cast from the graveyard via Jace, Vryn's Prodigy // Jace, Telepath Unbound’s −3 ability (the situation you described). If Brainstorm had instead been cast using flashback, Memory Lapse’s ruling notes that flashback would change the destination to exile instead.
citations: Jace, Vryn's Prodigy // Jace, Telepath Unbound

- Prismari Command then tries to resolve. Per Prismari Command ruling #1, if at least one of its chosen targets is still legal when it resolves, Prismari Command will resolve and do as much as it can. Per rule 608.2f, the multiple actions caused by Prismari Command (the “deal 2 damage” action and the “destroy target artifact” action) are processed together; they affect Duskworker simultaneously.
- Damage is processed into results (see 120.4c–d), and replacement/prevention effects that interact with those results are applied. If a regeneration effect created by Welding Jar is a replacement or prevention effect, rules about replacement and prevention effects (614.1, 615.1) and the procedure for choosing among multiple such effects (616.1f) would govern what happens next.

What’s missing and why that matters: the rules you supplied do not include the definition or procedural rules for “regenerate” (what event it replaces, what it does to damage marked on a permanent, whether it replaces a “destroy” event or prevents it, and the exact steps applied when both a destroy and damage event occur simultaneously). Without those specific regeneration rules, I can’t say whether the regeneration created by Welding Jar’s ability will cause Duskworker to survive Prismari Command’s destroy and 2 damage or what state Duskworker would be in afterward.

If you can provide the official rule text that defines “regenerate” (or the relevant comprehensive regeneration rule), I will apply it to the sequence above and give a definitive ruling about whether Duskworker survives and in what state.

Assumption noted: I assumed the Welding Jar activation resolved before Prismari Command (the activation was put on the stack in response and therefore resolves first). results.question: Armando controls [Mana Reflection] and taps [Pyromancer's Goggles] to add {R}{R}. They spend one mana to cast [Into the Fray]. Later in the phase they spend the other mana to cast [Galvanic Discharge]. Which one(s) are copied?
results.text: Both Into the Fray and Galvanic Discharge are copied. Mana Reflection causes the single activation of Pyromancer's Goggles to produce {R}{R}; each red mana produced is tracked by Pyromancer's Goggles’ effect, so spending one of those red mana on Into the Fray produces a copy of Into the Fray and spending the other red mana on Galvanic Discharge produces a copy of Galvanic Discharge.

results.question: Alden controls [Spark Double] and casts [Clone]. Alden would like to have Clone copy Spark Double, then they would like to apply the replacement effect Clone inherited from Spark Double and have it copy Spark Double again. If Alden has Clone copy Spark Double a total of four times, how many +1/+1 counters will Clone enter the battlefield with?
results.text:
Clone will enter the battlefield with one +1/+1 counter.

Reasoning: When Clone is made to enter the battlefield as a copy, copy effects are copiable effects applied as the object enters (see Layer 1a) [613.1a, 613.2a]. Copy effects can include exceptions that add counters as part of the copying process; Spark Double’s printed text makes such an exception (it “enters with an additional +1/+1 counter on it if it’s a creature”), so that is an exception to the copying process that would put a +1/+1 counter on an entering copy [Spark Double ruling #0, Spark Double ruling #6]. However, if a copy effect that included such an exception is applied and then another copy effect is applied afterward to the same entering object, the earlier exception’s additional effect does not happen (the later copy effect replaces the earlier one’s exception) [707.9e]. Replacement effects don’t repeatedly re-invoke themselves to generate additional copies or counters beyond what the final applied replacement chain produces [614.5].

Putting that together: if Alden has Clone copy Spark Double repeatedly so that Clone ends up having a chain of copy effects applied to it a total of four times, only the final copy effect that is actually applied as Clone enters can cause the “enters with an additional +1/+1 counter” exception to apply. Because that final copy effect is copying Spark Double (which grants just one such additional +1/+1 if the entering object is a creature), Clone enters with exactly one +1/+1 counter, not four.

If you care about counters copied from other abilities Spark Double copied, Spark Double’s ruling notes those may also apply (“plus any counters that will be put on it from abilities it copied and other abilities of other objects”) [Spark Double ruling #6]; my answer here concerns only the extra +1/+1 granted by Spark Double’s own exception and how repeated copying of that exception doesn’t stack [707.9e].

results.question: Ahmed casts [Bitter Ordeal], targeting Nico. At their first opportunity, Ahmed sacrifices their [Abandoned Outpost]. How many cards will Ahmed be able to exile from Nico's library?
results.text:
Answer: If Ahmed sacrificed Abandoned Outpost after casting Bitter Ordeal, Ahmed will exile one card from Nico’s library. If Ahmed sacrificed Abandoned Outpost before casting Bitter Ordeal, Ahmed will exile two cards from Nico’s library.

Reasoning and definitions:
- Gravestorm is the ability on Bitter Ordeal that reads in part “When you cast this spell, copy it for each permanent put into a graveyard this turn.” That means the number of copies created is determined at the time you cast Bitter Ordeal (Bitter Ordeal card text).
- Bitter Ordeal’s main effect is “Search target player’s library for a card and exile it. Then that player shuffles.” Each copy produced by Gravestorm is a separate instance of that instruction, so each (original spell and each copy) causes a separate search/exile (Bitter Ordeal card text).
- Therefore: if Abandoned Outpost was put into a graveyard before Ahmed cast Bitter Ordeal, Gravestorm will see one permanent put into a graveyard this turn and will copy Bitter Ordeal once, giving Ahmed the original plus one copy = two separate search/exile actions. If Abandoned Outpost was sacrificed only after Ahmed cast Bitter Ordeal, Gravestorm’s copy count was already determined with Abandoned Outpost not yet in the graveyard, so there are no copies and only the original Bitter Ordeal resolves, giving one search/exile.
- If Nico’s library doesn’t contain enough cards to satisfy the searches, a player searching a hidden zone “for a card” must find that many cards or as many as possible; likewise, effects that attempt to do something impossible do as much as possible ([701.23d], [609.3]).

Assumption note: I assumed the phrase “at their first opportunity” means the sacrifice happened after casting Bitter Ordeal (the first opportunity after the cast). If instead Abandoned Outpost was sacrificed before Ahmed began casting Bitter Ordeal, the answer switches to the second case above.

results.question: Autumn restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]'s last ability. They put a [Quilled Slagwurm] onto the battlefield as it resolves. Can it attack on their first turn?
results.text: Yes. Quilled Slagwurm can attack on Autumn’s first turn after Autumn restarts the game with Karn Liberated’s −14 ability. Summoning sickness means a creature can’t attack (or activate abilities with {T} or {Q} in their cost) unless that creature has been under its controller’s control continuously since that player’s most recent turn began (rule 302.6). Karn Liberated’s ability, when it restarts the game, causes permanents put onto the battlefield by that ability to be considered to have been under the starting controller’s control continuously since the beginning of that player’s first turn, and creatures among them “can attack” (Karn Liberated ruling #5). If any such permanent entered the battlefield tapped, it will untap during its controller’s first untap step (Karn Liberated ruling #6), so entering tapped won’t stop Quilled Slagwurm from being untapped and able to attack on that first turn.

results.question: Abel plays [Exotic Orchard]. What can it tap for if Nico controls only [Throne of Makindi] without any charge counters on it?
results.text:
Exotic Orchard can be tapped for one mana of any color: {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, or {G}. Exotic Orchard cannot be tapped for {C} (colorless). 

Definitions used
- “Could produce”: The type of mana a permanent could produce includes any type of mana an ability of that permanent would produce if that ability were to resolve at that time; ignore whether any costs of the ability could be paid [106.7].
- “Tap [a permanent] for mana”: To activate a mana ability of that permanent that includes the {T} symbol in its activation cost [106.12].

Why
- Throne of Makindi has an ability that reads “{T}, Remove a charge counter from this land: Add two mana of any one color” (card text). That ability is a mana-producing ability that would produce two mana of any one color if it resolved, so Throne of Makindi could produce mana of any of the five colors under the “could produce” definition [106.7]; also, mana abilities remain mana abilities even if the game state doesn’t allow them to actually produce mana [605.2].
- Exotic Orchard’s ability looks at the mana-producing abilities of lands an opponent controls without checking their costs, so Exotic Orchard can consider Throne of Makindi’s color-producing ability even though Throne of Makindi currently has no charge counters and thus can’t actually pay its remove-a-counter cost [Exotic Orchard ruling #4].
- Exotic Orchard can’t be tapped for colorless mana, so it can’t use Throne of Makindi’s “{T}: Add {C}” option to produce {C} for Exotic Orchard’s effect; only the five colored mana types are available [Exotic Orchard ruling #2].

Assumption: I assume the timing question is just what Exotic Orchard can be tapped for at the moment given Nico controls only Throne of Makindi with no charge counters. If Throne of Makindi’s state changed (for example, it actually had a charge counter), the set of mana it “could produce” would be the same in this interaction because costs are ignored when determining “could produce” [106.7].

results.question: Abraham controls [Drought] and [Derelor]. How many Swamps would they have to sacrifice in order to cast a [Virulent Wound]?
results.text:
Abraham must sacrifice two Swamps to cast Virulent Wound.

Why: Virulent Wound’s mana cost is {B} (Virulent Wound). Derelor makes black spells you cast cost an additional {B} (Derelor), so the spell’s total mana cost becomes {B}{B}. Drought requires you to “Sacrifice a Swamp” to cast a spell for each black mana symbol in that spell’s mana cost (Drought), so there are two black mana symbols and two Swamps must be sacrificed. This is determined when the spell’s total cost is locked in during casting and before payments are made (rule 601.2b; rule 601.2h). The Drought ruling gives the same kind of counting principle for multiple {B} symbols ([Drought ruling #2]).

Definitions and timing assumption: To cast means to take a spell from where it is, put it on the stack, and pay its costs (rule 601.2b). I’m assuming a normal casting timing where total costs (including cost increases and additional “Sacrifice a Swamp” costs) are determined before payment; if a different ordering of effects applied that changed the number of black mana symbols in the spell’s mana cost before the total cost was determined, that would change the number of required Swamps (see rule 601.2h).

results.question: Abram controls a [Blood Moon], a [Life and Limb], and a [Tropical Island], that entered the battlefield in that order. Is the Tropical Island a creature?
results.text:
I can’t answer definitively with only the provided rules: the context doesn’t include the rules that decide whether Blood Moon’s “Nonbasic lands are Mountains” effect removes Tropical Island’s Forest land type before Life and Limb could make it a creature, so it’s undecidable from the supplied material.

Definition of the key term: “Is a creature” means the permanent has the card type creature (see Creature). Relevant facts from the provided material: Life and Limb’s text makes all Forests “1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types” (Life and Limb and Life and Limb ruling #0 and #2), so a land that is a Forest would become a creature. Tropical Island’s card data shows it has the land subtypes Forest and Island (Tropical Island ruling #1 and 305.6). Blood Moon’s text says nonbasic lands are Mountains (Blood Moon), and Blood Moon ruling #3 notes that the effect doesn’t change names or supertypes but does not say whether it replaces or merely adds land subtypes; Blood Moon ruling #0 notes that a nonbasic land can lose an enters-the-battlefield ability before it triggers while Blood Moon is in effect.

What’s missing to decide this: the supplied rules do not include the comprehensive rules about continuous-effect interaction and layering (the rules that explain how two continuous effects that change an object’s subtypes or types interact, and whether wording like “Nonbasic lands are Mountains” replaces the land’s existing land types or adds Mountain). Because those layering/type-change rules aren’t present in the provided context, I can’t determine whether Tropical Island is still a Forest (and therefore a creature under Life and Limb) or whether Blood Moon has made it only a Mountain (so Life and Limb wouldn’t apply).

If you provide the rules on continuous-effect layers/type changes or an authoritative ruling that explains how Blood Moon’s “are Mountains” interacts with other effects that check for the Forest subtype, I can give a definitive answer.

results.question: Nixon has a [Southern Elephant] and a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters in their graveyard. Addison casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Nixon. What happens to the counters on the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave? Will Nixon know which manifested card is which?
results.text:
Skullbriar, the Walking Grave keeps its three +1/+1 counters when Addison exiles and then manifests Nixon’s graveyard cards; Addison (the caster of Ghastly Conscription) can look at the manifested cards and so will know which face-down permanent is Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, while Nixon will not be told which is which. 

Reasoning and definitions (short):
- Manifest: To manifest a card means to put that card onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2 creature; a face-down creature card that’s a creature card can be turned face up later for its mana cost (text from Ghastly Conscription). This is the action Ghastly Conscription carries out when it “manifest[s]” the exiled cards. (See Ghastly Conscription.)
- Ghastly Conscription exiles all creature cards from the target player’s graveyard into a face-down pile, shuffles that pile, then manifests those cards. The pile is shuffled to disguise which manifested creature is which, and after you manifest the cards you (the caster of Ghastly Conscription) can look at them. (See Ghastly Conscription ruling #0.)
- Normally counters don’t move with an object when it changes zones (counters cease to exist when an object moves zones; see rule 122.2) and an object that moves zones becomes a new object (see rule 400.7). 
- Skullbriar, the Walking Grave’s printed text and its rulings explicitly state a different result: “Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library,” and its ruling clarifies that Skullbriar, the Walking Grave retains all counters when it changes zones. Therefore when Skullbriar, the Walking Grave is exiled face down and then later manifested onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2, the three +1/+1 counters remain on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave. (See Skullbriar, the Walking Grave and Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1.)
- Note: Skullbriar, the Walking Grave still becomes a new object when it changes zones (see rule 400.7) and Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #4 explains that although the counters are retained, the object is a new object with no relation to its previous existence; effects that depend on a continuous condition tied to the previous existence may stop applying once it left the battlefield.

Timing/assumption: This explanation assumes the ordinary timing of Ghastly Conscription as written (exile into a face-down shuffled pile, then manifest). If the order of those steps were changed, you would apply the same card-specific retention language when Skullbriar, the Walking Grave moves zones.

results.question: Asa casts [Chatterstorm]. In response, Nico casts [Gather Specimens]. After everything resolves, Asa activates the second ability of [Homeward Path]. Who gains control of the token?
results.text:
Nico ends up controlling the Squirrel token. Gather Specimens causes the token created by Chatterstorm to enter the battlefield under Nico’s control, Homeward Path’s ruling says the owner of a token is the player under whose control it entered, and Homeward Path’s activated ability then gives each player control of the creatures they own — so Nico (who owns the token under that ruling) gains/retains control of it.

Reasoning and definitions:
- "Control": A permanent’s controller is, by default, the player under whose control it entered the battlefield [110.2b]. A control-changing effect that says a player "gains control" of something is a control-changing effect (applied in Layer 2) [613.1b].
- "Owner of a token": Normally, the rules state the player who creates a token is its owner [111.2]. However, the official ruling for Homeward Path says "The owner of a token is the player under whose control the token was put onto the battlefield" (Homeward Path ruling #1). That ruling is authoritative for interpreting Homeward Path’s ability and so applies here.
- Sequence in this game state (assumption: Nico’s Gather Specimens resolved before Chatterstorm resolved, per the question's timing): Nico cast Gather Specimens in response to Asa’s Chatterstorm, so Gather Specimens resolved before Chatterstorm resolved. When Chatterstorm resolved it created the 1/1 green Squirrel token(s). Gather Specimens’s replacement effect makes any creature that would enter the battlefield under an opponent’s control this turn enter under the controller of Gather Specimens instead (Gather Specimens; Gather Specimens ruling #3). That causes the token to enter the battlefield under Nico’s control.
- Because Homeward Path’s ruling says the owner of a token is the player under whose control it entered, Nico is the token’s owner (Homeward Path ruling #1). When Asa activates Homeward Path’s second ability ({T}: Each player gains control of all creatures they own), that effect gives each player control of creatures they own — Nico gains/retains control of the token (Homeward Path).

If you assume a different timing — e.g., Nico did not have Gather Specimens resolve before Chatterstorm resolved — then the token would enter under Asa’s control and (per the normal rule that the creator is the token’s owner [111.2]) Asa would be the owner; then Homeward Path’s ability would make Asa gain control of the token instead.

results.question: Aaliyah controls a [Squandered Resources] and a [Glacial Floodplain]. Nicolas controls [Blood Moon]. If Aaliyah sacrifices Glacial Floodplain to Squandered Resources, what type(s) of mana can it produce?
results.text: Squandered Resources will add one {R} (one red mana). Reasoning: Blood Moon makes nonbasic lands Mountains and causes them to lose their other land types and abilities and gain the ability “{T}: Add {R}” (Blood Moon ruling #2). Glacial Floodplain is a nonbasic land, so while Blood Moon is in effect Glacial Floodplain’s only mana-producing ability is “{T}: Add {R}” (Glacial Floodplain’s normal “{T}: Add {W} or {U}” is lost). Squandered Resources’s ability adds one mana of any type the sacrificed land could produce; “could produce” means any type an ability of that permanent would produce if that ability were to resolve at that time, taking into account replacement effects in any possible order (106.7). Therefore Glacial Floodplain could produce only {R} under Blood Moon, so Sacrificing Glacial Floodplain to Squandered Resources produces one {R}. (If Blood Moon were not in play, Glacial Floodplain could produce {W} or {U}, and Squandered Resources could add one {W} or one {U} accordingly.)

results.question: Neil controls [Willow Elf] enchanted with [Felidar Umbra]. Ainsley casts [Anger of the Gods]. What happens?
results.text:
Willow Elf survives. Neil (the controller of Willow Elf) chooses to apply Felidar Umbra’s umbra armor replacement: remove all damage from Willow Elf and destroy Felidar Umbra instead, so Willow Elf remains on the battlefield with no damage marked and is not exiled by Anger of the Gods. Other creatures still receive 3 damage from Anger of the Gods as normal.

Reasoning and details (key terms defined):
- "Umbra armor" (Felidar Umbra’s static ability) means “If enchanted permanent would be destroyed, instead remove all damage from it and destroy this Aura.” This effect is mandatory for Felidar Umbra and applies no matter why the enchanted creature would be destroyed (including lethal damage); see Felidar Umbra ruling #3 and Felidar Umbra ruling #4 and rule 702.89a. 
- Anger of the Gods deals 3 damage to each creature, and it has a replacement-style instruction: “If a creature dealt damage this way would die this turn, exile it instead” (Anger of the Gods ruling #0). Damage is processed in stages (damage is dealt, then processed into results, and replacement effects that interact with those results are applied) as summarized in rules 120.4b, 120.4c, and 120.4d.
- Both Felidar Umbra’s umbra armor and Anger of the Gods’ exile instruction are replacement effects that would modify what happens when Willow Elf would die, so both are attempting to modify the same event. When two or more replacement or prevention effects are attempting to modify the same event, the affected object’s controller chooses which to apply first (rule 616.1f). The affected object is Willow Elf, so Neil chooses.
- If Neil chooses Felidar Umbra’s umbra armor first, do as it says: remove all damage from Willow Elf and destroy Felidar Umbra. Because the damage is removed, Willow Elf no longer would die, so Anger of the Gods’ “exile instead” replacement does not apply to Willow Elf. Destroying Felidar Umbra puts that Aura into its owner’s graveyard as a state-based action (see rule 704.5m). The rest of Anger of the Gods’ effects on other creatures proceed normally.
- (Alternate, if Neil instead chose Anger of the Gods’ replacement first) If Neil chose to apply Anger of the Gods’ “exile instead” replacement, Willow Elf would be exiled rather than put into a graveyard. When Willow Elf leaves the battlefield, Felidar Umbra becomes unattached and would be put into its owner’s graveyard as a state-based action (rule 704.5m and 303.4c). In that line, Willow Elf would be exiled and Felidar Umbra would end up in its owner’s graveyard.

Assumption about timing: this explanation assumes Anger of the Gods has resolved and its damage-dealing event is being processed in the normal damage sequence; if damage or other effects happened in a different timing window the replacement-application timing rule (616.1f) still governs the choice.

results.question: Asa controls [Library of Leng] and is discarding a card due to [Azra Oddsmaker]'s ability. Can they put the discarded card on top of their library? If so, what happens?
results.text:
Yes. Asa may put the card being discarded on top of their library instead of into their graveyard; Library of Leng’s ability replaces the normal discard action with one that puts the card on top of the library. After that replacement, the card is on top of Asa’s library.

Reasoning and key definitions: A “discard” in this interaction is the normal discard action (moving a card from hand to graveyard) that the effect would cause; Library of Leng’s ability replaces that normal discard action with one that puts the card on top of the library instead of into the graveyard (Library of Leng ruling #7). Library of Leng cannot be used to replace discards that are costs (Library of Leng ruling #1) — however, the discard caused by Azra Oddsmaker’s ability is an effect of that ability (Azra Oddsmaker’s card text says “you may discard a card” as part of the ability), so it is not a cost and Library of Leng’s replacement ability can apply. If more than one card were discarded due to a single effect, Asa may decide for each discarded card whether to use Library of Leng’s ability and, if more than one card is put on top of the library, Asa chooses the order (Library of Leng ruling #5).

results.question: Noah controls [Compost]. Ainsley controls [Dune Beetle] and a token that was created as a copy of [Bogstomper]. Ainsley casts [Soulscour]. How many times does Compost trigger?

results.question: Albert, Brielle, and Campbell are playing a multiplayer game. Brielle controls [Stalking Leonin]. Albert casts [Worst Fears] to take control of Brielle's next turn. After Brielle begins their turn, can Albert see which player was chosen for the Stalking Leonin?
results.text:
Direct answer: The provided rules and rulings here don’t settle whether Albert can see which player Brielle secretly chose with Stalking Leonin after Albert begins controlling Brielle’s turn.

Why this is unresolved under the given material

- “Secretly choose an opponent” is the action required by Stalking Leonin’s triggered ability when Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield; Stalking Leonin’s ruling notes you may record that choice (for example, by writing the chosen player’s name on a piece of paper kept with Stalking Leonin) but does not state whether that recorded information is part of the game or who can see it ([Stalking Leonin ruling #0]).
- Worst Fears says “You control target player during that player’s next turn” and its ruling says that while controlling another player you “see all cards in the game that player can see” and you “make all decisions for them” ([Worst Fears], [Worst Fears ruling #0]).  723.1 likewise explains what “control a player during their next turn” means ([723.1]).
- 723.4 says that if information about an object in the game would be visible to the player being controlled, that information is also visible to the controller of the player; it also says the controller of a player can see that player’s hand and the face of any face-down creatures they control ([723.4]).

These statements together show that Albert can see anything Brielle would see that is a card or information about an object in the game. They do not, however, say whether a secret choice made when Stalking Leonin entered (or a note kept with Stalking Leonin recording that choice) counts as “information about an object in the game” that Brielle could see during her turn. Stalking Leonin’s ruling showing you may record the choice doesn’t say whether that recording becomes a visible game object, nor does Worst Fears’ ruling expressly extend visibility to non-card, nonstandard bookkeeping information created by a prior secret choice.

What’s missing to give a definitive ruling

- An explicit rule or ruling saying whether a secret choice recorded on a piece of paper “kept with” a card is considered an object or information in the game that the controlled player (and therefore the controller of that player) can see; or
- An explicit ruling that a controller of a player sees prior secret choices the controlled player made (or does not see them).

Because neither of those is present in the provided rules/rulings, I can’t definitively say whether Albert can see which opponent was secretly chosen for Stalking Leonin.

Assumption note: I’ve assumed the Stalking Leonin’s choice was made when Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield (as its text requires) and that Worst Fears’ control effect is in effect for the entire next turn (per 723.1). If an explicit ruling said that recorded secret choices are part of the game and visible to the controlled player, then Worst Fears’ controller would be able to see the chosen player; if an explicit ruling said recorded secret choices are private information that isn’t part of the game, then Worst Fears’ controller would not be able to see it.

results.question: Abdullah controls [Primal Vigor] and casts [Rescuer Sphinx], choosing to return Primal Vigor to their hand. How many +1/+1 counters will Rescuer Sphinx enter the battlefield with?
results.text: Rescuer Sphinx will enter the battlefield with one +1/+1 counter. Reason: Rescuer Sphinx’s “As this creature enters…” ability makes you choose to return a nonland permanent while Rescuer Sphinx is entering, and that returned permanent is removed before Rescuer Sphinx is on the battlefield with a +1/+1 counter, so Primal Vigor will not be on the battlefield to double the counters. Specifically, Rescuer Sphinx ruling #0 says you choose whether to return a nonland permanent and which one while Rescuer Sphinx is entering the battlefield, and no player may take actions between that choice and the time Rescuer Sphinx is on the battlefield with a +1/+1 counter; Rescuer Sphinx ruling #1 notes that a returned permanent won’t trigger abilities that would trigger when Rescuer Sphinx enters (showing the returned permanent has left the battlefield before those enter-related effects occur). Primal Vigor affects permanents that “enter the battlefield with” counters (Primal Vigor ruling #2), but because Primal Vigor is returned to hand as part of Rescuer Sphinx’s entering process, it isn’t on the battlefield to cause doubling. If Abdullah had not chosen to return Primal Vigor, Primal Vigor would double any counters Rescuer Sphinx entered with (so a normally one +1/+1 counter would become two), per Primal Vigor ruling #2.

results.question: Arturo uses [Vengeful Ancestor] to goad [Craw Wurm]. After it's been goaded, Nico uses [Brokers Confluence], causing Craw Wurm to phase out. On Nico's turn, what are Nico's legal combat choices?
results.text:
If Craw Wurm is still phased out when Nico reaches the declare attackers step, Nico may not attack with Craw Wurm (it’s treated as though it doesn’t exist). If Craw Wurm phases in before Nico declares attackers, then Craw Wurm is a goaded creature and Nico must declare Craw Wurm as an attacker this combat if it is able; in a two‑player game the “attack a player other than the goader” part is impossible and therefore does not add any extra choice, so Craw Wurm would be declared attacking Arturo if able.

Reasoning and definitions (short):
- Goad means a creature is given the goaded designation; a goaded creature “attacks each combat if able and attacks a player other than the controller of the permanent, spell, or ability that caused it to be goaded if able” ([701.15b]). Multiple players can goad the same creature, creating additional requirements ([701.15c]); the same player goingad the same creature again does nothing ([701.15d]). Vengeful Ancestor’s text is the source of the goad here (Whenever Vengeful Ancestor ... goad target creature) (Vengeful Ancestor).
- Phasing: a permanent that phases out becomes “phased out” and “is treated as though it does not exist” except where rules say otherwise; a phased-out permanent can’t affect or be affected and is removed from combat ([702.26b]). Brokers Confluence’s mode says “Target creature phases out. (Treat it and anything attached to it as though they don't exist until its controller's next turn.)” (Brokers Confluence).
- Because a phased-out permanent is treated as though it does not exist and is removed from combat, it cannot be declared as an attacker while phased out ([702.26b], [506.4]).
- Declaring attackers is a turn-based action with specific checks: the active player chooses which creatures they control will attack and must obey any “attacks if able” requirements when determining a legal declaration ([508.1a], [508.1d]); if defending players/planeswalkers/battles exist the active player must announce which player/planeswalker/battle each attacker is attacking ([508.1b]).
- Creatures can attack only opponents (and their planeswalkers/battles) within the attacker’s range of influence; in a two‑player game the only legal defending player for Nico’s creatures is Arturo ([801.3], [506.2]).

Timing note / assumption: The provided rules do not specify the exact moment a phased-out permanent becomes phased in on “its controller’s next turn.” Two plausible timings affect the answer:
- If Craw Wurm phases in before Nico’s declare attackers step, Craw Wurm is present and is a goaded creature, so Nico must declare Craw Wurm as an attacker this combat if it is able (and, in the two‑player case, that means attacking Arturo) ([701.15b], [508.1a], [508.1b], [801.3]).
- If Craw Wurm remains phased out through the declare attackers step, it is treated as not existing and Nico has no obligation (and no ability) to attack with it; Nico may attack (or not) with any other creatures as normal ([702.26b], [506.4], [508.1a]).

Because the question didn’t state exactly when Craw Wurm phases in on Nico’s turn, both outcomes above are legal depending on that timing.

If that permanent wouldn’t produce any mana under those conditions, there’s no type of mana it could produce. Applying that to these cards: Gaea's Cradle’s printed ability is “{T}: Add {G} for each creature you control.” With zero creatures, that ability would add zero {G}, so Gaea's Cradle wouldn’t produce any mana and thus Sylvok Explorer’s ability (“{T}: Add one mana of any color that a land an opponent controls could produce.”) has no color to choose and produces no mana (see also [106.5]).

results.question: Anson controls [Zirda, the Dawnwaker], [Sundial, Dawn Tyrant], and [Mobilized District]. How much does Anson have to pay to activate the second ability of Mobilized District?

Mobilized District’s text reduces that activation cost by {1} for each legendary creature and planeswalker you control; Anson controls two legendary creatures, Zirda, the Dawnwaker and Sundial, Dawn Tyrant, so that reduction is {2}, bringing the cost to {2} (Total Cost). Zirda, the Dawnwaker’s static ability reduces activation costs of abilities you activate that aren’t mana abilities by {2}, but Zirda, the Dawnwaker’s ruling clarifies “this effect can’t reduce the mana in that cost to less than one mana,” so Zirda, the Dawnwaker reduces the {2} cost by only {1}, leaving a final cost of {1} generic mana. The {1} is generic mana (a numerical symbol), so any type of mana that can pay generic mana may be spent to pay it.

Assumptions/definitions used:
- Activation Cost: everything before the colon in an activated ability’s text; it must be paid by the player activating the ability ([Activation Cost], [602.1a]).
- Generic mana: numerical symbols (such as {1}) represent generic mana ([107.4b]).
- Total Cost: the mana/activation cost plus cost increases minus cost reductions; calculate reductions and then apply Zirda, the Dawnwaker’s restriction ([Total Cost], [118.7]).

If you want the breakdown: start {4} (Mobilized District) → −{2} for two legendary creatures (Zirda, the Dawnwaker and Sundial, Dawn Tyrant) = {2} → Zirda, the Dawnwaker reduces up to {2} but may not reduce below {1}, so it reduces only {1} → final {1}.
