results.question: Andi controls [Karn Liberated], which has exiled an [Anvil of Bogardan]. They activate Karn Liberated's -14 ability, and restarts the game. How many cards will they draw during their first turn?
results.text:
Andi will draw two cards during their first turn: one from the normal draw step and one additional card from Anvil of Bogardan.

Reasoning: Karn Liberated’s restart-causing ability finishes resolving before the first turn and then puts the non‑Aura permanent cards it left in exile onto the battlefield under the ability’s controller’s control, and the controller of that ability is the starting player in the new game ([Karn Liberated ruling #4], [Karn Liberated ruling #2], [727.4]). That means Anvil of Bogardan will be on the battlefield under Andi’s control by the time Andi’s first draw step occurs. The draw step’s turn-based action makes the active player draw a card first ([504.1]). Anvil of Bogardan’s ability causes that player to draw an additional card “at the beginning of each player’s draw step” (Anvil of Bogardan card text), so Andi draws one more card that draw step. Therefore Andi draws one (normal draw) + one (Anvil of Bogardan) = two cards during their first turn’s draw step.

Assumption: I assume the question means cards drawn during Andi’s first turn (i.e., the draw step). The starting‑hand draws that occur when the new game begins are separate from draws during the turn ([Karn Liberated ruling #2]).

results.question: Nico controls [Drought]. How many Swamps would Ava have to sacrifice in order to cast [Beckon Apparition]?
results.text:
Ava must sacrifice one Swamp only if she chooses to pay Beckon Apparition’s {W/B} as {B}; if she pays that hybrid symbol as {W}, she sacrifices zero Swamps. 

Reasoning and definitions:
- Hybrid mana symbol: a hybrid symbol such as {W/B} is itself a colored symbol that can be paid with one mana of either named color; when a spell with a hybrid symbol is being cast, the caster announces the nonhybrid equivalent they intend to pay (definition and rule applied below). (See Symbol reference and rule 601.2b.)
- Drought’s text makes casting spells cost an additional “Sacrifice a Swamp” for each black mana symbol in their mana costs, so whether an extra Swamp must be sacrificed depends on whether the spell’s mana cost counts as containing a black symbol (Drought card text).
- When casting Beckon Apparition, which has mana cost {W/B}, the caster announces whether they will pay that hybrid symbol as {W} or as {B} (rule 601.2b). If Ava announces paying the hybrid as {B}, the announced nonhybrid equivalent includes one black mana symbol, so Drought imposes one “Sacrifice a Swamp” additional cost; if Ava announces paying the hybrid as {W}, the announced nonhybrid equivalent includes no black symbols, so Drought imposes no such additional cost. After those choices are made, the total cost (including any additional costs from Drought) is paid (rule 601.2h).

If you want the short practical line: choose how to pay the {W/B} — pay it as white to avoid sacrificing a Swamp, or pay it as black and sacrifice one Swamp.

results.question: Nico controls [Solemnity]. Aimee controls [Vizier of Remedies] and a tapped [Barrenton Medic]. Can Aimee untap Barrenton Medic with its own ability?
results.text:
No — Aimee can’t activate Barrenton Medic’s “Put a -1/-1 counter on this creature: Untap this creature” ability while Nico controls Solemnity. Solemnity’s text says “Players can’t get counters. Counters can’t be put on artifacts, creatures, enchantments, or lands,” so the required putting of a -1/-1 counter as the activation cost can’t happen; because that counter placement is a cost paid when you activate the ability, the cost is unpayable and the activation is not allowed.

Reasoning and key definitions: 
- Solemnity (the card) prevents putting counters on creatures (its printed text).
- An activated ability has a cost and an effect ([602.1]).
- The Barrenton Medic ruling ([Barrenton Medic ruling #0]) states that “You put the -1/-1 counter on Barrenton Medic as a cost. That means it happens when you activate the ability, not when it resolves.” Thus putting the -1/-1 counter is part of the activation cost.
- A player can’t pay a cost without having the necessary resources ([118.3]). Because Solemnity prevents putting counters on creatures, Aimee can’t perform that cost. 
- A player can’t begin to activate an ability that’s prohibited from being activated ([602.5]). Therefore Aimee can’t begin to activate Barrenton Medic’s untap ability while Solemnity is in effect.
- If Vizier of Remedies is also in play, Solemnity’s “can’t” effect takes precedence over effects that would otherwise change how many counters would be placed ([101.2a]), so Vizier of Remedies doesn’t allow the counter-placement cost to be paid while Solemnity is active.

Because the cost cannot be paid at the time of activation, Barrenton Medic’s ability can’t be activated and Barrenton Medic remains tapped.

results.question: Aislinn controls [Anointed Procession] and a [Skullmulcher]. They cast [Tempt with Reflections] targeting the Skullmulcher. Can Aislinn apply the devour replacement effect before the Anointed Procession replacement effect, sacrificing 1 creature to have each token enter with a +1/+1 counter?
results.text:
No. You cannot apply Skullmulcher’s devour replacement before Anointed Procession’s replacement. Anointed Procession’s replacement modifies the event of creating tokens (the outer event), and that replacement must be applied before replacement effects that modify how each token enters the battlefield (such as Skullmulcher’s devour). As a result, Tempt with Reflections will create twice as many Skullmulcher tokens under Aislinn’s control, and devour will then be applied separately as each Skullmulcher token enters; you may not sacrifice a single creature once and have that one sacrifice apply to multiple tokens entering, because the token-creation doubling happens first and each entering permanent’s devour choice is applied as it enters.

Definitions and reasoning
- Replacement effect: an effect that modifies how an event affects an object or player (rules discussion uses these as the things being chosen between). See rule process for multiple replacement effects [616.1g], [616.1].
- Self-replacement effect: a replacement effect that replaces part or all of a spell or ability’s own effect; such effects must be chosen in the replacement-effect ordering when they apply [614.15]. Skullmulcher’s devour is an enters-the-battlefield replacement effect that applies “as this creature enters” (see Skullmulcher ruling), so it is applied while that creature/token is entering [Skullmulcher ruling #0], [614.15].
- Creating tokens vs. entering the battlefield: creating a token is an event that contains the token’s entering-the-battlefield event; a replacement effect that modifies token creation (like Anointed Procession) must be applied before replacement effects that modify the token’s entering-the-battlefield event [616.1g]. That is why effects that double token creation are applied before enters-the-battlefield replacement effects.
- You can’t make one sacrifice serve for multiple entering permanents when replacement effects are applied in this order: the doubling of token creation by Anointed Procession happens first, then each token’s Skullmulcher devour is applied as that token enters, and you can’t choose the same object to change zones more than once when applying replacement effects that modify how one or more permanents enter the battlefield [614.13b]. Also Skullmulcher’s devour can’t devour creatures that enter at the same time as the Skullmulcher token itself [Skullmulcher ruling #0].

Assumption: I’m assuming the normal timing where Tempt with Reflections resolves and creates token(s). If you instead meant some other ordering of events, say so and I’ll analyze that specific timing.

results.question: Bailey controls [Pandemonium]. Anderson casts [Gray Ogre] and targets Bailey's [Jibbirik Omnivore] with the Pandemonium trigger. In response Chelsea casts [Incinerate] targeting Anderson causing them to lose the game. Will Bailey's creature die?
results.text:
Yes. Assuming Gray Ogre entered, Pandemonium’s triggered ability was on the stack, and Chelsea’s Incinerate resolved (making Anderson lose the game) before that triggered ability resolved, Bailey’s Jibbirik Omnivore will still be dealt damage by the Pandemonium trigger and will be put into its owner’s graveyard if that damage is lethal.

Reasoning and definitions (what I’m assuming):
- I assume the timeline is: Gray Ogre enters the battlefield → Pandemonium’s triggered ability is created and put on the stack → Chelsea casts Incinerate in response and Incinerate resolves, causing Anderson to lose the game → the Pandemonium triggered ability later resolves. If the timing were different (for example, the Pandemonium triggered ability resolved before Incinerate), the trigger would resolve while Anderson was still in the game; the conclusion about Jibbirik Omnivore’s fate would be the same because of the following rules.

- Triggered ability independence and controller/choice: Pandemonium’s triggered ability is controlled by Bailey even though Anderson (the creature’s controller) chooses whether to have the creature deal damage and chooses the target when the ability is put onto the stack (Pandemonium ruling #0). Once that triggered ability is on the stack, it exists and will resolve independently of what happens to its source or to Anderson (the source and the controller can change or leave the game without preventing the ability from resolving) (rule 113.7a).

- What happens if Gray Ogre or Anderson aren’t on the battlefield when the Pandemonium ability resolves: Pandemonium’s triggered ability doesn’t check Gray Ogre’s power until it resolves; if Gray Ogre is not on the battlefield when the ability resolves, the ability still deals damage equal to Gray Ogre’s power right before it left the battlefield (Pandemonium ruling #1). That means the trigger will still attempt to deal damage equal to Gray Ogre’s power even if Gray Ogre and/or Anderson are no longer in the game when the ability resolves.

- Damage processing and state-based actions: Damage dealt by the Pandemonium triggered ability will be processed (see the damage-processing step, rule 120.4c). If that damage causes Bailey’s Jibbirik Omnivore’s total damage marked to be greater than or equal to its toughness (Jibbirik Omnivore is a 3/2), a state-based action will put Jibbirik Omnivore into its owner’s graveyard (rule 704.5f and rule 704.1). Note that damage itself doesn’t “destroy” the creature; the state-based action of having toughness 0 or less or lethal damage is what puts it into the graveyard (rule 120.5 and rule 704.5f).

Putting that together: The Pandemonium triggered ability on the stack will still resolve even though Anderson lost the game in response (113.7a). When it resolves, it will use Gray Ogre’s power as appropriate even if Gray Ogre isn’t on the battlefield (Pandemonium ruling #1). If that resolution deals 2 damage (Gray Ogre’s power) to Bailey’s Jibbirik Omnivore, that damage equals Jibbirik Omnivore’s toughness and state-based actions will put Jibbirik Omnivore into its owner’s graveyard (704.5f, 120.4c). Therefore, Bailey’s Jibbirik Omnivore will die in this scenario.

If you want an even shorter summary: yes — the Pandemonium trigger still resolves and deals damage (using Gray Ogre’s last known power if needed), and lethal damage will cause Jibbirik Omnivore to be put into its owner’s graveyard by state-based actions.

results.question: Alice controls a [Life and Limb], a [Blood Moon], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What is the Saproling?
results.text:
I can’t give a definitive single final state with only the provided rules — the set is missing the rule that decides how to apply multiple continuous effects that change land subtypes in the same layer (timestamp/order-of-application for continuous effects). Because of that missing rule, there are two reasonable outcomes:

1) If the effect that makes the 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token a Forest land (Life and Limb) is the one that applies last, the token is a green 1/1 Saproling creature and a Forest land and therefore has the Forest land’s mana ability (“{T}: Add {G}”) (it entered as a land creature under the Life and Limb effect). This follows from the token-creation rule and Life and Limb’s text and ruling that Saprolings enter as land creatures and get the Forest subtype and related land characteristics ([111.3]; Life and Limb ruling #3; Life and Limb ruling #0; 305.6).

2) If the effect that makes nonbasic lands Mountains (Blood Moon) is the one that applies last, the 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token is still a green 1/1 Saproling creature (Life and Limb makes Saprolings creatures and Blood Moon does not remove creature types), but it will be a Mountain land instead of a Forest and will lose its other land types and land abilities and gain “{T}: Add {R}” as Blood Moon’s ruling says for nonbasic lands ([Blood Moon ruling #2]; Life and Limb ruling #0; 111.3).

What’s missing: the provided context does not include the rule that determines the relative application order (timestamp/order) for continuous effects that change types or subtypes in the same layer; that missing rule is required to pick between the two outcomes above. Because that rule isn’t in the supplied context, I must set answered = false.

Assumptions/definitions used:
- “1/1 Green Saproling Creature token” is the token created (tokens have characteristics defined by the creating effect) ([111.3]).
- A “Forest” is a basic land type that intrinsically has “{T}: Add {G}” ([305.6]).
- A “nonbasic land” is any land without the supertype Basic ([Nonbasic Land]; [Basic]).
- Life and Limb’s text makes Saprolings into Forest lands and into 1/1 green Saproling creatures (Life and Limb ruling #0 and ruling #3). Blood Moon makes nonbasic lands Mountains and strips their other land types and abilities while giving them “{T}: Add {R}” (Blood Moon ruling #2).

If you want a single, actionable ruling for play, give me which of Life and Limb or Blood Moon has the later timestamp (which entered most recently or otherwise applies last), and I’ll state the resulting characteristics of the 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token.

results.question: Anson controls [Mana Reflection] and [Deathrite Shaman]. They activate Deathrite Shaman's first ability, exiling a [Watery Grave] from Nola's graveyard. How much mana is produced?
results.text:
Anson produces two mana of a single color of Anson’s choice (two mana of the same color). The Deathrite Shaman ability would normally add one mana of any color; because Mana Reflection doubles what a permanent tapped for mana produces, that becomes two mana of the chosen color.

Reasoning and definitions:
- "To tap [a permanent] for mana" means to activate a mana ability of that permanent that includes {T} in its activation cost; that is what the phrase "tap ... for mana" refers to here [106.12b].
- Deathrite Shaman’s first ability is “{T}: Exile target land card from a graveyard. Add one mana of any color.” Because that ability includes {T} and its effect is to add mana, it is a mana-producing ability that adds one mana of any color (Deathrite Shaman).
- Mana Reflection’s text is authoritative: “If you tap a permanent for mana, it produces twice as much of that mana instead.” That causes a permanent you tap for mana to produce twice as much as it otherwise would (Mana Reflection; [Mana Reflection ruling #2]).
- When an effect increases the amount of mana produced by a spell or ability, any restrictions on the mana produced by that spell or ability apply to all mana produced (so the choice of color from Deathrite Shaman’s ability applies to both mana) [106.6a].
- The source of the mana is the activated Deathrite Shaman ability that produced it (rule on source of mana) [106.3].

Therefore, when Anson activates Deathrite Shaman’s first ability and exiles Watery Grave from Nola’s graveyard, Anson chooses a color and receives two mana of that color. Watery Grave’s identity or the colors Watery Grave could produce is irrelevant to the color-decision because Deathrite Shaman’s ability text simply says “Add one mana of any color.”

Assumption about timing: this answer assumes the normal resolution of Deathrite Shaman’s activated ability (you tap Deathrite Shaman, the ability resolves, you add mana). If somehow the ability were replaced or prevented from producing mana, the result could differ (see the cited rules above).

results.question: Alfredo controls [Magnetic Web] and is attacking with two [Knight Errant]s with magnet counters on them. Nico controls one [Soaring Drake] that also has a magnet counter on it. What are Nico's legal blocks?
results.text:
Soaring Drake must be declared blocking one of the attacking Knight Errant creatures this declare blockers step if Soaring Drake is able; Nico chooses which Knight Errant Soaring Drake blocks. 

Reasoning: Magnetic Web’s ability says “Whenever a creature with a magnet counter on it attacks, all creatures with magnet counters on them block that creature this turn if able,” so each attacking Knight Errant creates a requirement that all creatures with magnet counters (including Soaring Drake) block that specific attacking Knight Errant this turn if able (Magnetic Web). During the declare blockers step the defending player must obey blocking requirements to the maximum extent possible and may not leave more requirements unfulfilled than necessary (509.1; 509.1c). Because Soaring Drake can be declared to block at most one attacking creature, the maximum number of those “block that creature” requirements that can be obeyed for Soaring Drake is 1, so Nico must declare Soaring Drake to block one of the two attacking Knight Errant creatures (Nico chooses which one). Once declared, Soaring Drake becomes a blocking creature that is blocking the chosen Knight Errant (509.1g). 

If Soaring Drake is tapped, affected by a restriction that prevents it from blocking, or would have to pay a cost to block and Nico chooses not to pay that cost, Soaring Drake isn’t “able” to block and isn’t required to block (509.1a; 509.1b; 509.1d; 509.1c).

results.question: At the beginning of the game, Alianna announced [Zirda, the Dawnwaker] as their companion. During the game, Alianna cast [Glistening Goremonger] from their sideboard with [Wish]. Later, Alianna restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. What happens?
results.text:
Direct answer: When Alianna restarts the game with Karn Liberated, Glistening Goremonger (the card Alianna cast from their sideboard with Wish) will become part of Alianna's library as the new game begins. Zirda, the Dawnwaker (Alianna's announced companion) remains outside the game; Alianna may again reveal Zirda, the Dawnwaker as their companion during the new game's pregame if they choose and if their starting deck meets the companion restriction.

Why: Wish allows a player to play a card they own from outside the game that turn, so Glistening Goremonger was brought into the game from outside during the restarted game (Wish). Rule 727.2 says that when a game is restarted, cards that were brought into that game from outside the game become part of their owner's library when the new game begins (727.2). Karn Liberated's restart effect ends the prior game and causes the new game to begin (Karn Liberated ruling #0; 727.1), so Glistening Goremonger is put into Alianna's library for the new game.

Zirda, the Dawnwaker began the original game outside the game as a revealed companion and remained outside the game (Zirda, the Dawnwaker ruling #8; 103.2b; 702.139b). Because Zirda, the Dawnwaker was not brought into the game during the old game, it was not one of the cards that 727.2 moves into the new game's library; it stays outside the game. When the new game is set up, players may follow the pregame companion procedure again (103.2b), so Alianna may reveal Zirda, the Dawnwaker as a companion for the new game if applicable.

Assumption/clarification: This answer assumes Glistening Goremonger was indeed brought into the game from outside the game by Wish during the original game; the ruling about being put into the library on restart applies to cards brought into the game from outside (Wish; 727.2). If Glistening Goremonger had never been brought into the game (for example, if it had remained entirely in the sideboard and was never played), it would not be treated as a card that was “brought into the game” and thus would follow the normal pregame/starting-deck treatment instead (103.2a–b).

results.question: Amos controls [March of the Machines] and [Mycosynth Lattice] and casts [Lust for War] targeting their [Gilded Sentinel]. What will happen when Lust for War resolves?
results.text:
When Lust for War resolves, Lust for War will enter the battlefield attached to Gilded Sentinel, but because Mycosynth Lattice makes Lust for War an artifact and March of the Machines makes noncreature artifacts into artifact creatures, Lust for War becomes an Aura that is also a creature, so Lust for War can’t enchant anything; it becomes unattached at the next state-based actions check and is then put into its owner’s graveyard. 

Reasoning and definitions
- Lust for War is an Aura that enters the battlefield attached to the targeted creature when its spell resolves (Lust for War). 
- Mycosynth Lattice makes all permanents artifacts in addition to their other types (Mycosynth Lattice). That causes Lust for War to be an artifact as soon as it’s a permanent. 
- March of the Machines makes each noncreature artifact an artifact creature with power and toughness equal to its mana value (March of the Machines). Once Lust for War is an artifact permanent and is not a creature by its text, it is a noncreature artifact and becomes an artifact creature under March of the Machines. 
- An Aura that’s also a creature can’t enchant anything; such an Aura is unattached the next time state-based actions are checked and is then put into its owner’s graveyard as a second state-based action (Mycosynth Lattice ruling #0). 

So the timeline is: Lust for War resolves and enters attached to Gilded Sentinel; continuous effects from Mycosynth Lattice and March of the Machines immediately make Lust for War an artifact creature Aura; because an Aura that’s a creature can’t be attached as an Aura, Lust for War becomes unattached at the next state-based actions check and is then put into its owner’s graveyard.

If anything else changes the object’s characteristics or attachments between resolution and the state-based actions check, those changes would be applied before the unattaching and putting into the graveyard, but the ruling above governs the normal outcome.

results.question: Avery controls [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathan casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics after Turn to Frog resolves?
results.text:
Direct answer: After Turn to Frog resolves, Wayward Angel is a blue Frog creature with no abilities and has base power and toughness 1/1, and it then gets +3/+3 from its threshold, so its final power/toughness is 4/4. It is not white (it’s blue), and it has no flying, vigilance, trample, or the “At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature” triggered ability.

Reasoning and steps (rules used):
- “Characteristics” are determined by starting with the actual object (the printed Wayward Angel card) and then applying all applicable continuous effects in layers (see 613.1g).  
- Turn to Frog’s effect makes the targeted permanent “lose all abilities and becomes a blue Frog with base power and toughness 1/1.” That effect sets the creature’s base power and toughness to 1/1 and makes it blue Frog when it resolves (see Turn to Frog ruling #1 and Turn to Frog ruling #5).  
- Effects that set a creature’s base power and toughness are applied in layer 7b; other power/toughness modifications (such as “gets +3/+3”) are applied later in the layer series (see 613.4b and 613.1g). Turn to Frog therefore sets Wayward Angel’s base P/T to 1/1, and Wayward Angel’s threshold “gets +3/+3” then modifies that, producing a final P/T of 4/4 (Turn to Frog overwrote any earlier base-setting effects, per Turn to Frog ruling #1).  
- Wayward Angel’s threshold text makes Wayward Angel black while the threshold condition is met (Wayward Angel ruling #0). Turn to Frog makes the creature blue; continuous effects that change the same characteristic are applied in layers/timestamp order, so the later (Turn to Frog) color-setting effect results in Wayward Angel being blue after Turn to Frog resolves (613.1g; see also the Turn to Frog ruling #5 example showing Turn to Frog producing a blue creature).  
- Turn to Frog causes the creature to “lose all abilities,” so Wayward Angel loses its abilities (flying, vigilance), loses trample granted by threshold, and loses the triggered upkeep ability granted by threshold. (See Turn to Frog ruling #5 that the affected permanent will have no abilities; Turn to Frog ruling #3 notes that abilities gained after Turn to Frog resolves are kept, which is why the removal is tied to the moment Turn to Frog’s effect is applied.)

Timing note/assumption: This answer assumes Turn to Frog resolves while Wayward Angel’s controller still has seven or more cards in their graveyard (so the threshold condition is satisfied both before and after Turn to Frog resolves). If the graveyard count changes so the threshold condition no longer holds at the moment effects are applied, the +3/+3 and the threshold-granted pieces would not be present.

results.question: Aubrey casts [Shahrazad]. As the subgame begins, Aubrey wins the die roll. Can Aubrey choose to play second?
results.text: Yes. Shahrazad’s ruling says the subgame randomly chooses which player gets to choose who goes first; that chosen player then decides who is the starting player (who takes the first turn). So if Aubrey was the randomly chosen player, Aubrey may choose an opponent to be the starting player and therefore play second. Reasoning: rule 729.2 says a subgame’s starting player is determined randomly as the subgame begins, and rule 103.1 says the player chosen to take the first turn is the starting player (the player who takes the first turn). Shahrazad ruling #3 specifically treats the subgame’s random determination as randomly choosing which player chooses who goes first or draws first, so the randomly chosen player can choose not to be the starting player and instead have another player start.

results.question: Ainsley's [Morality Shift] resolves, in what order do they put cards in their graveyard?
results.text:
Ainsley chooses the order. When Morality Shift resolves, Ainsley arranges the cards being put into her graveyard in any order, then her library is shuffled.

Reasoning: Morality Shift’s resolution causes multiple cards to be put into the same graveyard at the same time; when that happens the owner may arrange those cards in any order ([404.3]). The card’s official ruling explicitly confirms this: “You can choose the order of the cards being placed into the graveyard.” ([Morality Shift ruling #1]). After the cards are placed, a player’s graveyard is a single face-up pile whose order normally can’t be changed ([404.2]).

results.question: Autumn, Bethany, and Chaim started playing a multiplayer game. Chaim lost the game, and then Autumn restarted the game with [Karn Liberated]. Will Autumn draw a card on the first turn of the restarted game?
results.text:
Yes. Autumn will draw a card on the first turn of the restarted game. The ability of Karn Liberated that restarted the game makes the controller of that ability the starting player for the new game, and in a multiplayer game the starting player does not skip the draw step, so Autumn (who restarted the game with Karn Liberated) will draw during that draw step.

Definitions and reasoning
- “Restarting the game” means the current game immediately ends and all players who were in that game when it ended begin a new game following the normal game-start procedures, except that the starting player in the new game is the player who controlled the spell or ability that restarted the game (Karn Liberated). See [727.1a] and [Karn Liberated ruling #2].
- The draw step’s turn-based action is that the active player draws a card immediately after the draw step begins (this action doesn’t use the stack). See [504.1] and [703.4d].
- Because any player who left the game before Karn Liberated’s ability restarted it isn’t involved in the new game, Chaim (who lost and left before the restart) won’t be in the new game. See [Karn Liberated ruling #9].
- Therefore Autumn is the starting player of the new multiplayer game (controller of Karn Liberated’s restart ability) and, under multiplayer rules, the starting player does not skip the draw step of their first turn. See [727.1a], [Karn Liberated ruling #2], and [800.7].

Assumption: I’m assuming the question means the first turn of the new game that began when Autumn used Karn Liberated’s −14 ability; if the timing were meant differently, say a separate extra turn effect after the restart, the same draw-step rules above would be applied to that turn’s draw step instead.

results.question: Addison casts [Virulent Wound], targeting Natalee's [Memnite]. In response, Natalee casts [Resounding Roar] on the Memnite. What happens at the end of the turn?
results.text:
Answer: Natalee’s Memnite ends up in Natalee’s graveyard during the cleanup step, and Natalee gets a poison counter from Virulent Wound.

Reasoning and definitions:
- Resounding Roar gives the targeted creature +3/+3 until end of turn (Resounding Roar).  That makes Natalee’s Memnite a 4/4 (base 1/1 +3/+3). (I assume Resounding Roar resolves before Virulent Wound because Natalee cast Resounding Roar in response to Addison casting Virulent Wound.)
- When Virulent Wound resolves, it puts a -1/-1 counter on the targeted creature and creates the ability “When that creature dies this turn, its controller gets a poison counter” (Virulent Wound).
- After Virulent Wound resolves, Natalee’s Memnite is 3/3 (1/1 +3/+3 then one -1/-1 counter). It is not put into a graveyard at that moment.
- At cleanup, all “until end of turn” and “this turn” effects end simultaneously (703.4p, 514.2). Resounding Roar’s +3/+3 ends, so Natalee’s Memnite becomes a 0/0 (1/1 minus the one -1/-1 counter).
- A creature with toughness 0 or less is put into its owner’s graveyard by state-based actions (704.5f). That is when Natalee’s Memnite is put into Natalee’s graveyard (it “dies” that turn).
- Because Virulent Wound specified “When that creature dies this turn, its controller gets a poison counter,” and the creature is put into a graveyard on the same turn Virulent Wound resolved, Natalee gets a poison counter (Virulent Wound ruling #0).

Key term definitions:
- “Until end of turn” effect: an effect that lasts until the cleanup step of the current turn and ends during that cleanup step (703.4p, 514.2).
- “Dies” / “is put into a graveyard”: for this interaction, “dies this turn” means the creature is put into a graveyard from the battlefield during the same turn Virulent Wound resolved (Virulent Wound; 704.5f).

Timing note: I assumed the spells resolved in the order implied (Resounding Roar resolves before Virulent Wound because it was cast in response). If instead Resounding Roar somehow failed to resolve before Virulent Wound, the outcomes could differ (for example, the -1/-1 counter might immediately make Natalee’s Memnite die before any +3/+3 is applied).

results.question: Amaris, Blaine, and Clyde begin a multiplayer game. In Amaris's upkeep, they use [Leyline of Anticipation], several [Simian Spirit Guide]s and [Desperate Ritual]s, and [Goblin Charbelcher] to kill Blaine. Does Amaris draw a card for the turn?
results.text: Yes. Amaris will still draw a card on their draw step. The draw step is the turn-based action that occurs when the draw step begins, and the active player draws a card immediately (draw step = rule 703.4d; drawing a card this way doesn’t use the stack = rule 504.1). When Blaine loses the game as a result of Amaris’s actions, Blaine leaves the game (rule 104.5) and multiplayer games can continue after one or more players leave (rule 800.4), so Amaris’s turn continues to its draw step unless Amaris’s action caused all of Amaris’s opponents to leave the game. If Amaris’s action did cause all of Amaris’s opponents to leave the game, Amaris would immediately win instead of proceeding to the draw step (rule 104.2a). Note that triggered abilities that trigger when a player loses the game will trigger when Blaine leaves (rule 603.9), but those triggers do not prevent the draw step from happening for the remaining active player in the normal case above. Definitions: “draw step” — the turn step that begins with the active player drawing a card immediately (rules 703.4d and 504.1). “Losing the game” — a player leaves the game as a result of losing the game (rule 104.5).

results.question: Allyson controls [Ice Cauldron]. Nico controls [Suppression Field]. Allyson activates Ice Cauldron's first ability with X=1, paying {C}{C}{C}. On Allyson's next turn, they activate Ice Cauldron's second ability. How much mana do they add?
results.text:
Allyson adds {C}{C}{C} (three colorless mana) to her mana pool when she activates Ice Cauldron’s second ability. Definition: A “mana ability” is an activated or triggered ability that produces mana (see rule 605.1).

Why: Suppression Field’s static ability makes activated abilities cost {2} more to activate unless they’re mana abilities, so when Allyson activated Ice Cauldron’s first ability with X = 1 she paid {1} for X plus the extra {2} from Suppression Field, for a total of {C}{C}{C} spent to activate that ability. Ice Cauldron’s first ability tells you to “note the type and amount of mana spent to pay this activation cost,” and Ice Cauldron “counts only mana spent on it” (so it noted the actual mana spent: {C}{C}{C}). When Allyson later activates Ice Cauldron’s second ability, it “Add[s] this artifact’s last noted type and amount of mana,” so it adds {C}{C}{C}. (Suppression Field does not increase the cost of activating Ice Cauldron’s second ability because that ability is a mana ability and Suppression Field doesn’t affect mana abilities.) Also note the added mana may be spent only to cast the last card exiled with Ice Cauldron, per Ice Cauldron’s text.

If you want the shortest takeaway: you get three colorless mana ({C}{C}{C}).

results.question: Anya activates [Deceptive Landscape]. Before that resolves Nico casts [Aven Mindcensor]. When Anya is resolving Deceptive Landscape's ability, they find [Panglacial Wurm] in the top four cards of their library. Can they cast it?
results.text: No — not if Anya already “found” Panglacial Wurm among the top four cards. Deceptive Landscape’s search is replaced by Aven Mindcensor’s replacement (so Anya is searching the top four cards of her library) [701.23f; Deceptive Landscape; Aven Mindcensor]. Panglacial Wurm’s special ability lets you cast it while you’re searching your library, but only if you cast it before you find any cards with the search effect; if you only realize Panglacial Wurm after you’ve found it among the cards, it’s too late to cast it this way [Panglacial Wurm ruling #5; Panglacial Wurm]. If Anya had chosen to cast Panglacial Wurm while still in the process of searching (i.e., before finding any card from the top four), she could do so and would follow the normal casting rules (pay costs, put the spell on the stack) [Panglacial Wurm ruling #1; Panglacial Wurm]. Note also that if Anya casts Panglacial Wurm during the search, Panglacial Wurm can’t be “found” by that search effect afterwards [Panglacial Wurm ruling #4].

results.question: Aimee controls a manifested [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Noah casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. After that resolves, Aimee turns Wayward Angel face up. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics afterwards?
results.text:
After Wayward Angel is turned face up, Wayward Angel is a black Frog creature with power/toughness 4/4 and it has trample and “At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature.” Wayward Angel does not have flying or vigilance and is not white.

Reasoning (short): A face-down Wayward Angel is a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, types, or abilities while face down (see rule 708.2). When Turn to Frog resolved while Wayward Angel was face down, that continuous effect applied to Wayward Angel and remains in effect after Wayward Angel is turned face up (see rule 708.8). When Wayward Angel is turned face up, its copiable values revert to its printed/copied values (Wayward Angel’s normal, printed characteristics) and then continuous effects are applied in layers and by timestamp (see rules 707.2 and 613.1, and timestamp handling in 613.7). Turn to Frog’s effect has an earlier timestamp (it resolved before Wayward Angel was turned face up), and Wayward Angel’s Threshold static effect begins applying only once Wayward Angel is face up (so it has a later timestamp). In the power/toughness layer (layer 7) Turn to Frog sets base power/toughness to 1/1, and then Wayward Angel’s Threshold gives +3/+3, yielding 1/1 +3/+3 = 4/4 (see 613.1g and Turn to Frog ruling #1). For color and types, Turn to Frog made Wayward Angel blue Frog earlier, and Wayward Angel’s Threshold (which makes Wayward Angel black and gives the +3/+3, trample, and the upkeep-triggered ability) applies afterward and sets the color to black (so Wayward Angel is black, not white; see Wayward Angel ruling #0 and 613.7 for timestamp ordering). For abilities, Turn to Frog removed all abilities when it resolved, but Wayward Angel’s Threshold grants trample and the upkeep-triggered ability after that; abilities gained after Turn to Frog resolved remain (Turn to Frog ruling #3), so those Threshold-granted abilities are present, while Wayward Angel’s printed flying and vigilance are not (they were removed by Turn to Frog and not re-granted by Threshold).

If you want the fully step-by-step layer/timestamp walkthrough, say so and I’ll list each applied effect in order.

results.question: Bobbie has 1 life and controls a phased-out [Angel of Sanctions] that exiled Conrad's [Rotted Hystrix]. Alana casts [Lava Axe], targeting Bobbie. What happens as Bobbie loses the game?
results.text:
When Bobbie loses the game, Bobbie’s phased-out Angel of Sanctions leaves the game and Conrad’s Rotted Hystrix returns to the battlefield immediately under Conrad’s control. The return is the one-shot effect tied to Angel of Sanctions leaving and does not go on the stack.

Reasoning and definitions
- “Leaves the game”: When a player leaves the game, all objects owned by that player leave the game and effects giving that player control of objects end; these things happen immediately (rule 800.4a; see also rule 405.6h about such actions not using the stack). 
- “Phased-out permanent”: A permanent that is phased out. Phased-out permanents owned by a player who leaves the game also leave the game (rule 702.26k). 
- Application here: Bobbie owns the phased-out Angel of Sanctions, so when Bobbie leaves the game Angel of Sanctions leaves the game (800.4a and 702.26k). Angel of Sanctions’s one-shot effect that returns the card it exiled causes Conrad’s Rotted Hystrix to be put onto the battlefield when Angel of Sanctions leaves the game; that return isn’t put on the stack and happens as part of the Angel of Sanctions-leaving event (Angel of Sanctions ruling #4). Thus Conrad’s Rotted Hystrix immediately returns to the battlefield under Conrad’s control as Bobbie leaves the game.

Assumption about timing
- I assume Lava Axe resolves and the resulting state causes Bobbie to lose and leave the game; the rest follows as described. If the loss happened for another simultaneous reason, the same “player leaves the game → owned objects leave the game → exiled card returns” sequence applies per the cited rules.

results.question: Aubrey controls [Mycosynth Lattice]. Natalia controls [Watchwolf] enchanted with [Favorable Destiny]. Aubrey casts [Opportunistic Dragon] and takes control of Favorable Destiny. What will happen after Opportunistic Dragon's ability resolves?
results.text:
Aubrey will gain control of Favorable Destiny; Favorable Destiny stays attached to Natalia's Watchwolf but loses all of its abilities, so it will not grant Watchwolf +1/+2 or shroud while Opportunistic Dragon remains on the battlefield.

Why: Mycosynth Lattice makes permanents into artifacts, so Favorable Destiny is a legal target for Opportunistic Dragon's triggered ability (see Mycosynth Lattice and Opportunistic Dragon). When Opportunistic Dragon's enters-the-battlefield triggered ability resolves, Aubrey gains control of the targeted permanent (Favorable Destiny) and that permanent “loses all abilities” for as long as Opportunistic Dragon remains on the battlefield (see Opportunistic Dragon). A control-changing continuous effect like that is applied as a control change (Layer 2) [613.1b]. Opportunistic Dragon's ruling confirms the control effect continues even if the stolen permanent loses all abilities or changes controllers later; the control effect only ends when Opportunistic Dragon leaves the battlefield (Opportunistic Dragon ruling #1).

Practical result: Favorable Destiny is now controlled by Aubrey and remains attached to Natalia's Watchwolf. Because Favorable Destiny has been made to “lose all abilities” by Opportunistic Dragon's continuous effect, Favorable Destiny's text (“Enchanted creature gets +1/+2 as long as it's white” and “Enchanted creature has shroud as long as its controller controls another creature”) no longer functions while Opportunistic Dragon remains on the battlefield, so those bonuses and shroud do not apply to Natalia's Watchwolf. (Separately, Mycosynth Lattice makes permanents colorless, so Watchwolf is not white under Mycosynth Lattice; even if Favorable Destiny still had abilities, the +1/+2 condition would not be met.)

results.question: Adelaide casts a [Keldon Champion]. In response, Nico casts [Hallow], targeting the Keldon Champion. When Adelaide attacks with the Keldon Champion that turn, will the damage be prevented?
results.text: No. Hallow’s prevention will not stop damage dealt later by Keldon Champion when it attacks that turn. Hallow (“Prevent all damage target spell would deal this turn. You gain life equal to the damage prevented this way.”) targeted the Keldon Champion spell on the stack, so it creates a prevention “shield” that watches for damage that that spell object would deal this turn. “Prevent” means what damage will not be dealt, and prevention effects act like shields that watch for a damage event (definition of prevent and prevention effects) [Prevent, 615.1]. When the Keldon Champion spell resolves it becomes the permanent Keldon Champion; the creature’s later combat damage is damage dealt by the Keldon Champion permanent (and its abilities), not damage dealt by the spell object on the stack. When a shield checks the source at the time damage would be dealt, it rechecks the source’s properties and won’t prevent the damage if the source no longer matches (for example, it’s no longer the same spell) [609.7b, 615.9]. Because the source at combat damage time is the Keldon Champion permanent rather than the Keldon Champion spell, Hallow’s shield does not match and so the combat damage is not prevented. (If the Keldon Champion spell itself somehow dealt damage while it was still a spell on the stack, Hallow could prevent that damage; Keldon Champion’s printed triggered ability deals damage when the creature enters the battlefield as a permanent, so Hallow won’t stop that either) [Keldon Champion, Hallow].

results.question: Amelia attacks with [Wildfire Eternal], which isn't blocked. As the trigger resolves, can they choose to suspend [Shivan Meteor]?
results.text:
No — you can’t suspend Shivan Meteor while Wildfire Eternal’s triggered ability is resolving. Wildfire Eternal’s ability resolves and gives you the opportunity to cast an instant or sorcery from your hand without paying its mana cost, but you don’t have priority while that ability is resolving, and suspending is a special action you may take only when you have priority.

Reasoning and definitions (grounded in the provided rules):
- Suspend: “Suspend N—[cost]” is an alternative action that lets you pay the suspend cost and exile the card with time counters; that action doesn’t use the stack (rule 702.62a). A card is “suspended” if it’s in exile and has time counters on it (rule 702.62b). Shivan Meteor’s suspend-specific ruling confirms exiling with suspend isn’t casting and doesn’t use the stack (Shivan Meteor ruling #3). 
- Special action / timing: Exiling a card from your hand using suspend is a special action you may take any time you have priority, but only if you could begin to cast the card (rule 116.2f and rule 702.62a; see also Shivan Meteor ruling #1 about when you can suspend). 
- Resolving abilities and priority: While a spell or ability is resolving, no player has priority, even if the resolution instructs players to make choices or take actions (rule 117.2e). Wildfire Eternal’s ruling says the ability resolves before combat damage is dealt and you must cast the spell at that time if you wish to cast one without paying its mana cost (Wildfire Eternal ruling #1). 

Putting that together: during the resolution of Wildfire Eternal’s triggered ability you do not have priority (117.2e), so you cannot perform the special action of exiling Shivan Meteor with suspend (116.2f, 702.62a). Shivan Meteor’s suspend action is explicitly not casting and can’t be done in place of the casting permission granted by Wildfire Eternal while that ability is resolving (Shivan Meteor ruling #3; Wildfire Eternal ruling #1).

results.question: Nadia has cast a [Gather Specimens] earlier in the turn. Ashley controls a [Peacewalker Colossus] that is currently a creature due to its own ability, and casts a [Clever Impersonator], choosing to have it copy Peacewalker Colossus. What happens?

Clever Impersonator enters the battlefield under Ashley’s control as a noncreature artifact Vehicle that is a copy of Peacewalker Colossus (it has Peacewalker Colossus’s printed power/toughness and printed abilities such as Crew and the “{1}{W}: Another target Vehicle you control becomes an artifact creature until end of turn” ability), so Gather Specimens does not cause it to enter under Nadia’s control.

Reasoning: A copy effect makes the entering object acquire the copiable values derived from the printed text of the chosen permanent (name, mana cost, color indicator, type line, rules text, power/toughness, etc.). Other effects — including effects that have changed the chosen permanent’s types or otherwise made the chosen permanent a creature — are not copied (they’re “non-copy effects”) (see rule 707.2). Clever Impersonator copies exactly what is printed on the chosen nonland permanent and doesn’t copy non-copy effects that have changed that permanent’s types or whether it’s a creature (see Clever Impersonator ruling #2). Therefore, even though Peacewalker Colossus is currently a creature due to a temporary effect, Clever Impersonator will enter as a copy of the printed Peacewalker Colossus (an artifact Vehicle with printed 6/6 and the printed abilities) but not as a creature. Because Clever Impersonator is not entering as a creature, Gather Specimens’s replacement effect (“If a creature would enter the battlefield under an opponent’s control this turn, it enters under your control instead”) does not apply to this entering permanent (see Gather Specimens ruling #3, which frames how Gather Specimens applies to creatures entering).

If instead Peacewalker Colossus were itself printed as a creature (or the copy effect explicitly included copying the current creature status as part of the copying process), then Gather Specimens could apply; the provided rules and rulings above are the basis for the answer.

results.question: Aubrey controls a [Gaea's Liege], [Rhonas the Indomitable], and 1 [Forest]. Noel controls 5 Forest. Can Aubrey attack with the Gaea's Liege and Rhonas the Indomitable?
results.text:
Yes. Aubrey can attack with both Gaea's Liege and Rhonas the Indomitable by declaring Gaea's Liege as an attacker first, then declaring Rhonas the Indomitable.

Definition: A creature is "attacking" once it has been declared as an attacker during the declare attackers step (the active player declares attackers one creature at a time and chooses a defending player for each). See rules below for how this matters.

Why this is legal, step by step:
- Gaea's Liege’s power while attacking is equal to the number of Forests the defending player controls, which is 5 here, so Gaea's Liege would be a 5/5 once it is declared as an attacker (Gaea's Liege). 
- Rhonas the Indomitable’s printed restriction is "Rhonas can't attack or block unless you control another creature with power 4 or greater" (Rhonas the Indomitable). The official ruling clarifies you do not have to attack with that other creature for Rhonas to be allowed to attack; you only need to control such a creature (Rhonas the Indomitable ruling #1).
- During the declare attackers step the active player chooses which creatures will attack and declares them one at a time; when a creature is declared as an attacker it becomes tapped and is treated as attacking (508.1a, 508.1f, 802.3b). The active player must check restrictions when declaring attackers (508.1c). Because the active player can declare Gaea's Liege as an attacker first, Gaea's Liege becomes attacking and thus becomes a 5/5; at that point Aubrey controls another creature with power 4 or greater, so the active player can legally declare Rhonas the Indomitable as an attacker afterwards.

Timing note: If Aubrey attempted to declare Rhonas the Indomitable as an attacker before declaring Gaea's Liege (so Gaea's Liege were still a 1/1 at that moment), that declaration would violate Rhonas the Indomitable's restriction and be illegal; an illegal declaration is reversed (733.1). Declaring Gaea's Liege first avoids that problem.

results.question: Ariyah casts [Stonewood Invocation] targeting [Skeletal Crocodile], and then attacks with the Skeletal Crocodile. Noah blocks it with a [Baron Sengir], which has gained infect due to their [Phyresis] and indestructible due to their [Valorous Stance]. What happens at the end of the turn?
results.text:
Skeletal Crocodile will be put into its owner’s graveyard at end of turn because it ends the turn with five -1/-1 counters that reduce its toughness to 0 or less. Whether Baron Sengir is also put into its owner’s graveyard at that time can’t be determined from the provided rules (the usual rule that lethal marked damage causes a creature to be put into its owner’s graveyard is not included in the excerpt).

Reasoning and assumptions

What “infect” means here: Infect is a keyword that makes damage to creatures be applied as -1/-1 counters and makes damage to players be given as poison counters (see rule 702.90 and 702.90c). This is why Baron Sengir’s infect causes counters instead of marked damage on the thing it damages.

What happens during combat (grounded in the provided rules and card text):
- Stonewood Invocation’s text is “Target creature gets +5/+5 and gains shroud until end of turn.” That makes Skeletal Crocodile a 10/6 for the turn while Stonewood Invocation’s effect exists (Stonewood Invocation).
- Phyresis’s text is “Enchanted creature has infect,” so Baron Sengir has infect while enchanted (Phyresis).
- Valorous Stance’s text can grant indestructible until end of turn, which prevents damage and “destroy” effects from destroying that creature while the effect lasts (Valorous Stance).
- When Skeletal Crocodile and Baron Sengir deal combat damage to each other, the damage is processed into results (see rule 120.4c and 120.4d). Because Baron Sengir has infect, the damage Baron Sengir deals to Skeletal Crocodile is applied as five -1/-1 counters on Skeletal Crocodile rather than as marked damage (702.90c). Skeletal Crocodile’s 10 damage to Baron Sengir is dealt as normal damage (120.3 / 120.4c).
- After those results are applied, Skeletal Crocodile (which was 10/6 while the +5/+5 applied) has five -1/-1 counters on it and therefore is a 5/1 while Stonewood Invocation still applies.

What happens at end of turn (what we can conclude from the provided rules):
- Stonewood Invocation’s +5/+5 and Valorous Stance’s indestructible both end at end of turn (they’re “until end of turn” effects; card texts cited above). The five -1/-1 counters placed by Baron Sengir’s infect remain on Skeletal Crocodile; counters are not removed merely because a temporary buff ends (the counters were created as the result of the damage event).
- With Stonewood Invocation gone, Skeletal Crocodile’s base 5/1 minus five -1/-1 counters leaves its toughness 0 or less. The provided state-based-action rule says “If a creature has toughness 0 or less, it’s put into its owner’s graveyard” (704.5f). Therefore Skeletal Crocodile is put into its owner’s graveyard at end of turn.

What is not settled by the provided rules

The provided excerpt does not include the state-based-action text that says a creature with damage marked on it equal to or greater than its toughness is put into its owner’s graveyard. Because that specific state-based-action text is not in the supplied rules, I cannot lawfully conclude from the given material whether Baron Sengir (which had 10 damage marked on it while it was indestructible) will be put into its owner’s graveyard when Valorous Stance’s indestructible ends. If you want a definitive ruling about Baron Sengir dying after indestructible ends, I need the rule that describes what happens to creatures that have damage marked on them equal to or greater than their toughness (the usual state-based-action about lethal damage).

Assumption note: I assumed normal simultaneous combat damage resolution (damage dealt and then processed into results during the damage event). If you intended a different timing (for example if some effect changed between damage dealing and end of turn), say so and I’ll re-evaluate.

results.question: Ariel casts [Prismari Command], with both modes targeting Nico. Will they be able to copy it with [Chef's Kiss]?
results.text:
Yes. Chef's Kiss can target Prismari Command as cast with both chosen modes targeting Nico, and Chef's Kiss will copy Prismari Command and then reselect new targets at random for each instance of “target” in the spell’s rules text (for both the original spell and the copy). 

Definition (modal): A spell is modal if it has two or more options in a bulleted list preceded by instructions to choose one or more options; each option is a mode. Choosing modes (and any targets required by those modes) is part of casting the spell. [700.2] [601.2c]

Reasoning: When Ariel cast Prismari Command, Ariel chose two modes and (for any mode that requires a target) announced the appropriate target(s) as part of casting the spell. [700.2] [601.2c] Prismari Command as cast therefore has multiple instances of the word “target” but all of those instances target the same player, Nico. Chef's Kiss can target “target spell that targets only a single permanent or player.” The authoritative ruling for Chef's Kiss says that if a spell has multiple instances of the word “target,” but all of them target the same permanent or player, that spell is a legal target for Chef's Kiss; in that case a new target will be reselected at random for each instance of the word “target” in the spell’s text, and the same is true for the copy. [Chef's Kiss ruling #4] 

Note: Normally a copy copies the original spell’s modes and targets, because copies copy those decisions, but Chef's Kiss’s effect then causes targets to be reselected at random for both the original spell (now controlled by the Chef's Kiss controller) and the copy. [707.10] 

Assumption about timing: I assume Ariel chosen both Prismari Command modes that require targets and named Nico for each during casting. If one chosen mode required no target, that mode would simply not add a target and Chef's Kiss’s interaction would still follow the ruling above for the remaining target instances. [601.2c]

results.question: Alejandra owns a face-down [Progenitus] in exile. Nicolas uses [Ruin Processor] to put Progenitus into Alejandra's graveyard. Where does Progenitus move to?
results.text: Progenitus is revealed and shuffled into Alejandra's library. Reasoning: Ruin Processor’s ability attempts to put a card an opponent owns from exile into that player's graveyard; you may choose Alejandra’s face-down Progenitus for that effect (Ruin Processor). However, Progenitus has a replacement effect that reads “If Progenitus would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, reveal Progenitus and shuffle it into its owner’s library instead” (Progenitus). That replacement effect applies to the event “would be put into a graveyard from anywhere,” so the attempt by Ruin Processor to put Progenitus into Alejandra’s graveyard is replaced by revealing Progenitus and shuffling Progenitus into Alejandra’s library. Because Progenitus was face down in exile, revealing is part of the replacement effect before Progenitus is shuffled into Alejandra’s library (see the similar example in [701.24g]).

results.question: Aurora controls a [Gaea's Liege] and 3 [Snow-Covered Forest]s. Nico controls a [Reverence] and 1 Snow-Covered Forest. Can Aurora attack with the Gaea's Liege?
results.text:
Yes. Aurora can declare Gaea's Liege as an attacker against Nico.

Reasoning: The declaration of attackers is the step in which the active player checks for restrictions that say a creature “can’t attack” and determines which creatures may be declared as attackers [508.1c]. Reverence’s text is such a restriction: “Creatures with power 2 or less can’t attack you” (Reverence). Gaea's Liege’s power while it isn’t attacking is equal to the number of Forests Aurora controls (Gaea's Liege). Aurora controls three Snow-Covered Forests, and Snow-Covered Forest is a Forest (Snow-Covered Forest; 305.6), so Gaea's Liege’s power at the time of declaration is 3, which is greater than 2 and therefore not prevented by Reverence. After Gaea's Liege is declared as an attacker, its power will change (while attacking it’s equal to the number of Forests the defending player controls), but that post-declaration change doesn’t retroactively make the declaration illegal because the restriction check occurs during the declaration of attackers [508.1c]. The defending player used for Gaea's Liege’s “while attacking” characteristic is the player it’s attacking (Nico) [802.2a].

results.question: Ari controls [Village Survivors] and [Vodalian Soldiers] and has 6 life. Nyla controls [Norn's Annex]. If Ari attacks with Vodalian Soldiers, paying 2 life, will it become tapped?
results.text:
Yes. Vodalian Soldiers will be tapped when Ari declares it as an attacker.

Reasoning: Declaring attackers causes the active player to tap the chosen creatures as part of that action (508.1f). Norn's Annex imposes a cost to attack that the attacking creature’s controller pays “as attackers are being declared” (Norn's Annex ruling #0), and optional or required costs to attack are chosen and then paid after creatures are tapped (508.1g, 508.1h). Ari has 6 life, so Ari may pay 2 life (119.4b) to satisfy Norn's Annex. Village Survivors’s ruling explains the timing explicitly: tapping to attack happens just before any required costs to attack are paid, and if paying such a cost causes the attacker’s controller to drop below 6 life, their tapped attackers will have vigilance but remain tapped for that combat (Village Survivors ruling #0). For completeness, vigilance means attacking doesn’t cause creatures with vigilance to tap (702.20b), which is why gaining vigilance earlier would normally prevent tapping, but the timing here (tap first, pay life second) means Vodalian Soldiers is already tapped and stays tapped for the combat.

results.question: Amari has [Phyrexian Hulk] and [The Mimeoplasm] in their graveyard. Amari casts [Rise of the Dark Realms] to return both to the battlefield. Can they have The Mimeoplasm enter the battlefield as a copy of Phyrexian Hulk?
results.text:
No. The Mimeoplasm can’t exile Phyrexian Hulk as part of its “As The Mimeoplasm enters” choice when both cards are being returned to the battlefield at the same time by Rise of the Dark Realms, so it can’t enter as a copy of Phyrexian Hulk in that situation.

Reasoning: Rise of the Dark Realms returns all creature cards from all graveyards onto the battlefield under your control, so Phyrexian Hulk and The Mimeoplasm would be entering the battlefield at the same time. The Mimeoplasm’s ability is an “as . . . enters” effect that exiles two creature cards from graveyards in order to have The Mimeoplasm enter as a copy of one of them (you choose which card it copies and which determines the +1/+1 counters). Rule [614.13a] says that while applying an effect that modifies how a permanent enters the battlefield, you can’t choose the object that will become that permanent or any other object entering the battlefield at the same time as that object as one of the objects to be moved. The given example in [614.13a] is directly analogous: you can’t exile a creature card that is itself entering the battlefield at the same time. Therefore The Mimeoplasm can’t exile Phyrexian Hulk as one of the two cards as it enters and so can’t enter as a copy of Phyrexian Hulk in this simultaneous-return scenario. If there were other creature cards in graveyards that are not also entering the battlefield at the same time, The Mimeoplasm could exile those and enter as a copy of one of them instead (see The Mimeoplasm’s card text and [The Mimeoplasm ruling #2] and [The Mimeoplasm ruling #3]).

results.question: Autumn casts [Time Stretch]. Can they choose to skip both extra turns with [Time Vault]?
results.text:
No. Autumn can’t use Time Vault to skip both extra turns granted by Time Stretch; at most one of those extra turns can be skipped with Time Vault.

Reasoning: Time Stretch gives the targeted player two extra turns after this one (see Time Stretch). Extra turns are added one at a time (rule 500.7). A “skip [turn]” effect is a replacement effect that is applied as a turn would begin (rules 614.10 and 614.1); Time Vault’s text and ruling say that the choice to skip is made as that turn would begin and only if Time Vault is tapped at that time, and if you choose to skip that turn Time Vault untaps before anything else happens in the next turn (Time Vault ruling #1). Therefore, if Autumn uses Time Vault’s “If you would begin your turn while this artifact is tapped, you may skip that turn instead. If you do, untap this artifact.” choice to skip the first extra turn, Time Vault will untap before the following extra turn begins, so it won’t be tapped at the beginning of the second extra turn and its skip option can’t apply to that second extra turn. (If Autumn instead declines to skip the first extra turn and Time Vault is still tapped at the beginning of the second extra turn, Autumn could then choose to skip that second extra turn.)

Assumption: I assume the normal timing where the two extra turns from Time Stretch are the next two turns to be taken by Autumn after the current turn; the same conclusion holds because extra turns are added one at a time (rule 500.7). If the timing of when the extra turns occur were different, the ruling about when the skip choice is made (Time Vault ruling #1) still governs each turn’s beginning.
