- Later, when Averie casts a spell, Averie may untap Pristine Angel due to Pristine Angel’s triggered ability (“Whenever you cast a spell, you may untap this creature.”). Once Pristine Angel is untapped, its static ability “As long as this creature is untapped, it has protection from artifacts and from each color” produces a continuous effect giving protection from black (Pristine Angel).
- Continuous effects that grant or remove abilities are applied in timestamp order (613.11). The “loses protection from black until end of turn” effect started when Cephalid Snitch’s ability resolved earlier; the “has protection … while untapped” effect begins only when Pristine Angel becomes untapped later. Under timestamp order (613.11), the later effect (the untap-caused protection) would be applied after the earlier “loses protection” effect, so the final game state would be that Pristine Angel has protection from black.
- Whether that final game state makes Pristine Angel an illegal target for Mob when Nico tries to cast Mob depends on how “protection” is defined with respect to targeting and target legality. Target legality and checks on resolution are governed by 608.2b (a spell checks whether its targets are legal when it resolves). But the provided rules do not include the rule that defines protection and how it affects targeting, so we cannot complete the analysis.

Missing rules needed to answer: the rule(s) that define protection (what protection from a color prevents, e.g., whether it prevents being targeted by spells of that color) and any authoritative ruling about how “loses protection” interacts with continuous static abilities. If you provide the rule(s) that define protection (or an official ruling showing that protection from a color prevents being targeted by spells of that color), I can finish the ruling using 608.2b and 613.11 and the card texts.

results.question: [Counterspell] is on top of the stack targeting my [Divination]. When everyone passes priority, what resolves first, and does Divination still resolve?
results.text:
Counterspell resolves first. When Counterspell resolves, it follows its instruction “Counter target spell,” so it counters Divination; Divination is removed from the stack and doesn’t resolve (it’s put into its owner’s graveyard).

Reasoning and definitions — assume no other actions occur before resolution: when all players pass in succession, the top object on the stack resolves ([117.4], [405.5], [608.1]). A spell is a card on the stack ([112.1]), and the controller of a resolving spell follows its instructions in the order written ([608.2c]). Counterspell’s instruction “Counter target spell” therefore counters the targeted Divination when Counterspell resolves. To “counter” means to cancel the spell: it doesn’t resolve and is put into its owner’s graveyard ([701.6a]).

Timing note: this answer assumes Counterspell is currently the top (last-added) object on the stack and everyone passes with no further actions. If, instead, Divination somehow left the stack or became an illegal target before Counterspell resolved, then Counterspell would attempt to resolve but couldn’t counter a nonexistent or illegal target; the specific outcome would depend on that different timing or game state change.

results.question: My [Charging Rhino] has trample and is blocked by [Vampire Nighthawk], which has deathtouch. How much combat damage do I have to assign to the blocker before I can trample the rest over to the player?
results.text: Assign 1 damage from Charging Rhino to Vampire Nighthawk; the remaining 3 damage from Charging Rhino can be assigned to the defending player. Reasoning: Trample requires the controller of an attacking creature with trample to assign lethal damage to the creature(s) blocking it before assigning any excess to the player (see rule 702.19b). Deathtouch means any nonzero amount of damage dealt to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered lethal for the purposes of determining excess damage, so only 1 point of damage from Charging Rhino needs to be assigned to Vampire Nighthawk to satisfy the “lethal damage” requirement (see rule 702.2c). Definitions: Deathtouch — any nonzero amount of damage dealt to a creature by a source with deathtouch is treated as lethal damage for checking excess damage (rule 702.2c). Trample — a keyword ability that modifies how an attacking creature assigns combat damage; its controller must assign lethal damage to blocking creatures before assigning any remaining damage to the player or planeswalker being attacked (rule 702.19b). Assumptions and notes: This answer assumes Vampire Nighthawk has no damage already marked on it and no other creatures are assigning damage to Vampire Nighthawk at the same time; if Vampire Nighthawk already has damage marked on it equal to or exceeding its toughness, you wouldn’t need to assign any damage to Vampire Nighthawk and could assign all of Charging Rhino’s damage to the defending player (see rule 702.19b, which says to take into account damage already marked on the creature, and rule 120.6, which explains damage marked on a creature persists until cleanup).

results.question: I have [Monastery Swiftspear] on the battlefield and I cast [Shardless Agent]. When its cascade ability puts a noncreature spell onto the stack, does Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger before or after that cascaded spell resolves?
results.text:
Monastery Swiftspear's prowess will trigger and resolve before the cascaded spell cast via Shardless Agent resolves.

Reasoning: A triggered ability is one that has a trigger condition and an effect ([603.1]). Prowess means “Whenever you cast a noncreature spell, this creature gets +1/+1 until end of turn” ([702.108a]); Monastery Swiftspear also clarifies that any noncreature spell you cast causes prowess to trigger ([Monastery Swiftspear ruling #1]). Shardless Agent's cascade ability triggers when you cast Shardless Agent and, if you cast the exiled nonland card, that exiled spell is put onto the stack above Shardless Agent ([Shardless Agent ruling #1]). When you cast that exiled noncreature spell, Monastery Swiftspear's prowess triggers; Monastery Swiftspear's rulings state that prowess “goes on the stack on top of the spell that caused it to trigger” and will resolve before that spell ([Monastery Swiftspear ruling #2]). Putting this together, the stack (top to bottom) will be: Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger(s) → the exiled noncreature spell cast via Shardless Agent → Shardless Agent. Therefore Monastery Swiftspear's prowess resolves first, giving the +1/+1 before the cascaded spell resolves.

(If the cascaded card is a creature, Monastery Swiftspear's prowess does not trigger per [Monastery Swiftspear ruling #1].)

results.question: My opponent's [Grizzly Bears] has 2 damage marked on it. Do state-based actions make it die before my [Lightning Bolt] resolves?
results.text: No. State-based actions will not destroy Grizzly Bears before Lightning Bolt resolves. State-based actions are automatic game checks that happen whenever certain conditions are met and do not use the stack; they’re performed each time a player would get priority (see rules [704.1], [704.2], [117.5]). However, state-based actions are not checked during the resolution of a spell or ability, so they “pay no attention to what happens during the resolution” of that spell (see rule [704.4]). Assuming Lightning Bolt is currently resolving: Lightning Bolt will deal 3 damage to Grizzly Bears as part of its resolution, and that damage is processed and marked on Grizzly Bears (see rules [120.4c] and [302.7]). After Lightning Bolt finishes resolving, state-based actions are then checked and, because the total damage marked on Grizzly Bears is now 5 (2 existing + 3 from Lightning Bolt) which is greater than or equal to Grizzly Bears’s toughness, Grizzly Bears is destroyed as a state-based action (see rules [302.7] and [120.6]). If instead you meant “before I cast Lightning Bolt” (i.e., before you would receive priority to cast it), the game would perform state-based actions first and Grizzly Bears would already be destroyed if it had lethal damage at that moment (see rule [117.5]).

results.question: It's my upkeep. My [Phyrexian Arena]'s beginning-of-upkeep trigger and my opponent's own beginning-of-upkeep trigger both want to go on the stack. Who chooses the order, and when exactly do they trigger?
results.text:
Direct answer: Both abilities trigger when your upkeep begins; you put Phyrexian Arena’s triggered ability onto the stack first (you’re the active player), then your opponent puts their triggered ability onto the stack, so your opponent’s triggered ability will be on top and will resolve before Phyrexian Arena’s. 

Why: A triggered ability is one written as “[When/Whenever/At] [trigger condition or event], [effect]” and it automatically triggers when its trigger event happens (definition: triggered ability) [603.1][603.2b]. When a phase or step begins, abilities that trigger “at the beginning of” that phase or step (for example, Phyrexian Arena’s “At the beginning of your upkeep…” trigger) trigger at that time and are put onto the stack the next time a player would receive priority [500.6][603.3b]. The upkeep step has no turn-based actions and the abilities that triggered at the beginning of the upkeep are put onto the stack before the active player receives priority [503.1a][117.3a].

Who orders them: If multiple triggered abilities have triggered since the last time players received priority, the game places them on the stack using APNAP order: each player, in active-player, nonactive-player (APNAP) order, puts the triggered abilities they control onto the stack in any order they choose (first those whose trigger conditions aren’t other abilities triggering on the stack, then the rest) [603.3b][101.4]. Because it’s your upkeep you are the active player, so you put Phyrexian Arena’s triggered ability onto the stack first in whatever order you choose for your triggered abilities, then your opponent puts their triggered ability(s) onto the stack in whatever order they choose; the abilities put on later will be on top of the stack and resolve first [603.3b][101.4].

Additional notes: If either triggered ability contains a “may” option, it still goes on the stack when it triggers; the controller decides whether to use the option when the ability resolves [603.5]. If more than two players are involved, the same APNAP procedure applies (active player first, then each other player in turn order) rather than assuming a two-player table [101.4][603.3b].

results.question: I cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, then copy that spell with [Fork]. Once everything resolves, how many copies of the card end up back in my hand?
results.text:
One card — only the original sorcery with buyback goes back to your hand; the copy created by Fork returns nothing.

Reasoning and definitions
- Buyback: As defined by rule 702.27a, Buyback is an additional cost you may pay as you cast a spell, and “If the buyback cost was paid, put this spell into its owner’s hand instead of into that player’s graveyard as it resolves.” Paying that additional cost happens while casting the spell (see rule 601.2f). 
- Copying a spell: Rule 707.10 says to copy a spell means to put a copy of it onto the stack; a copy of a spell isn’t cast and has no spell card associated with it. Fork’s rulings make this concrete: Fork puts a copy on the stack that is not a card (Fork ruling #10) and the copy is not considered to have been cast (Fork ruling #9). Fork’s ruling #8 explicitly states that if you copy a spell for which Buyback was paid, “you get nothing back since the copied spell does not have a card to give you.”

Putting that together: you paid the buyback cost when casting the original sorcery with buyback (601.2f, 702.27a), so when the original resolves it is returned to your hand instead of going to the graveyard (702.27a). The Fork copy is only a spell on the stack with no card to return, so it can’t put a card into your hand (707.10; Fork ruling #8; Fork ruling #10). Therefore exactly one card ends up back in your hand — the original card.

Assumption: I’m assuming you cast the sorcery with buyback from your hand and paid its buyback as part of casting it; if the spell were being cast from a different zone or without buyback paid, the outcome could differ.

results.question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?
results.text:
No — you will not get a token. You may exile Lightning Bolt with Mimic Vat’s imprint-triggered ability when the manifested face-down card dies, but because Lightning Bolt is an Instant (a nonpermanent card) Mimic Vat cannot create a token that’s a copy of it; activating Mimic Vat’s {3}, {T} ability in that situation will not put a token onto the battlefield.

Why: Mimic Vat’s ruling explains that if the creature that died was actually an instant or sorcery card that had been manifested, Mimic Vat may exile a nonpermanent card, but you can’t create a token that’s a copy of a nonpermanent card — “No token is created in this case” ([Mimic Vat ruling #0]). Mimic Vat’s second ability can be activated even when nothing is exiled, and if no valid card is exiled when that ability resolves no token is created ([Mimic Vat ruling #6]). For reference, Lightning Bolt is an Instant card (card data), so it is a nonpermanent in this interaction.

Definitions: “Nonpermanent card” here means a card that is not a permanent (for example, an Instant like Lightning Bolt). Mimic Vat ruling #0 treats an instant or sorcery that was manifested and then died as a nonpermanent card for the purposes of Mimic Vat’s abilities.

If you want the full interaction spelled out: when the face-down manifested Lightning Bolt dies, Mimic Vat’s triggered ability may exile Lightning Bolt’s card. Later, when you pay {3} and tap Mimic Vat to activate its create-a-copy ability, the ability won’t create a token because the exiled card is a nonpermanent (Lightning Bolt); the rules explicitly say no token is created in that case ([Mimic Vat ruling #0]).

results.question: My [Fiend Hunter]'s enters-the-battlefield ability is on the stack, about to exile a creature. I copy that ability with [Lithoform Engine] and target a second creature. Both get exiled. When Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, do both come back?
results.text: Yes — both creatures return to the battlefield when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield. Linked abilities are a pair where one ability causes actions (here, an enters-the-battlefield ability that exiles cards) and the other ability directly refers to those actions or cards; the second ability refers only to cards exiled by the first (definition: linked abilities). Fiend Hunter has an enters-the-battlefield ability that may exile another target creature and a leaves-the-battlefield ability that returns the exiled card; those two abilities are linked (see 607.1 and 607.2a and Fiend Hunter). When you copy Fiend Hunter’s enters-the-battlefield ability with Lithoform Engine, that copy is also linked to Fiend Hunter’s leaves-the-battlefield ability; if the leaves-the-battlefield ability refers to “the exiled card,” it refers to each card exiled by the original ability and the copy (see Lithoform Engine ruling #4 and 607.3). Therefore, if both the original and the copied enters-the-battlefield abilities resolve and exile two creatures, both of those exiled creatures will be returned when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield. Assumption: this answer assumes both the original and copied enters-the-battlefield abilities resolved and exiled their targets before Fiend Hunter left the battlefield. If Fiend Hunter left the battlefield before its enters-the-battlefield ability resolved, Fiend Hunter’s leaves-the-battlefield ability would trigger and do nothing, and the later resolution of the enters-the-battlefield ability would exile a creature indefinitely (see Fiend Hunter ruling #0).

results.question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?
results.text:
No — the exiled creature stays exiled. Phasing Banishing Light with Teferi's Protection does not cause Banishing Light to “leave the battlefield,” so the “until Banishing Light leaves the battlefield” condition hasn't occurred and the creature does not return.

Reasoning: Phasing means a permanent is treated as though it doesn't exist while it’s phased out, but phasing does not actually change the permanent’s zone or controller (it doesn’t leave the battlefield) and phasing in simply makes it phased in again (see rules 702.26d and 702.26c). Teferi's Protection’s ruling explicitly says that one-shot effects waiting “until [this] leaves the battlefield,” such as that of Banishing Light, won’t happen when a permanent phases out, so Banishing Light phasing out does not end the exile created by Banishing Light (see Teferi's Protection ruling #21 and the Banishing Light card text).

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?
results.text:
Yes. Your opponent can target Emrakul, the Promised End with Counterspell while Emrakul, the Promised End is on the stack, and if Counterspell resolves and counters Emrakul, the Promised End the triggered ability that was put on the stack when you cast Emrakul, the Promised End still exists and will resolve (so you still gain control of the targeted opponent during that player’s next turn and then that player takes an extra turn), unless that triggered ability’s target becomes illegal before it resolves.

Reasoning and definitions
- “Protection from instants” (brief definition): protection stops being targeted by instant spells and abilities from instant cards only while the object with protection is on the battlefield. Emrakul, the Promised End’s protection from instants therefore does not stop it from being targeted while it is on the stack. (Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #2; Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #1.)
- Triggered ability and the stack: The phrase on Emrakul, the Promised End — “When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn. After that turn, that player takes an extra turn.” — is a triggered ability that is created when you cast Emrakul, the Promised End and functions while that triggered ability is on the stack. That triggered ability is separate from the Emrakul, the Promised End spell on the stack. (603.1a)
- Targeting Emrakul, the Promised End on the stack: Because protection from instants applies only while Emrakul, the Promised End is on the battlefield, an instant such as Counterspell may legally target the Emrakul, the Promised End spell while it is on the stack. (Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #2; Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #1.)
- What happens if the spell is countered: If Counterspell resolves and counters the Emrakul, the Promised End spell on the stack, that does not remove the triggered ability that was already created and put on the stack when you cast Emrakul, the Promised End. Abilities on the stack are not spells and aren’t countered by spells that counter only spells; the triggered ability will still attempt to resolve. When that triggered ability resolves, targets are checked for legality; if the targeted opponent is still a legal target, the effect (you gain control of that opponent during that player’s next turn, then that player takes an extra turn) will happen. (113.9; 608.2b; 603.1a.)

Assumption about timing
- I’m assuming the opponent cast Counterspell in response to the triggered ability after you cast Emrakul, the Promised End but while the Emrakul, the Promised End spell was still on the stack. If instead Counterspell were cast after the triggered ability resolved (i.e., after you already gained control during that player’s next turn), the timeline and results would differ accordingly.

Multiplayer note
- The same interactions apply in multiplayer: Counterspell can target Emrakul, the Promised End on the stack, and the triggered ability that targets an opponent will still resolve later unless that chosen opponent becomes an illegal target before the ability resolves. (See Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14 if multiple player-control effects interact.)

results.question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
results.text: Yes — Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor can be a legal cascade hit, but you can cast only whichever face has a mana value less than your cascade spell’s mana value. Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor is a card with mana value 2, so cascade will stop on it if your cascade spell’s mana value is greater than 2. When you’re given the option to cast that exiled card, you may choose to cast either the Valki, God of Lies face or the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor face, but you may cast that face for free only if the resulting spell’s mana value (the mana value of the face you would cast) is less than your cascade spell’s mana value. Concretely: you may cast Valki, God of Lies (the front face, mana value 2) for free if 2 is less than your cascade spell’s mana value; you may cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor (the back face, mana value 7) for free only if 7 is less than your cascade spell’s mana value (which is normally not the case if cascade stopped on the card because of Valki’s front-face mana value).
citations: Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16
Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
results.text:
Direct answer: You will control one of your opponent’s turns (their next turn only), you will get a second Emrakul, the Promised End as a token permanent, and copying the Emrakul, the Promised End spell does not create another “When you cast this spell” trigger.

Why: • “Copy” means putting a copy on the stack; a copy of a spell isn’t cast. That is what happens when Lithoform Engine’s ability creates a copy of Emrakul, the Promised End’s triggered ability and when Lithoform Engine’s ability copies the Emrakul, the Promised End spell. See rule [707.10] and [Lithoform Engine ruling #6]. • A copy of a permanent spell that resolves becomes a token permanent with the characteristics of that spell, so copying the Emrakul, the Promised End spell will produce a second Emrakul, the Promised End permanent (a token) when that copy resolves. See rule [111.13]. • Because the copied Emrakul, the Promised End spell was not cast, copying the Emrakul, the Promised End spell does not cause another “When you cast this spell” trigger to be created. See [707.10] and [Lithoform Engine ruling #6]. • When you copied Emrakul, the Promised End’s cast trigger with Lithoform Engine you put a second instance of that triggered ability on the stack. Each of those triggered abilities, when they resolve, will create the control-for-next-turn effect and will create an extra turn for the targeted player after that turn. Emrakul, the Promised End’s rulings make two points that apply: multiple player-controlling effects that affect the same player overwrite each other (the last-created control effect is the one that actually causes you to control the target player’s next turn), while each ability’s effect will create an extra turn. See [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14]. • If both trigger instances target the same opponent and both resolve before that opponent’s next turn, you will end up with two extra turns created for that opponent (extra turns are added one at a time; see [500.7]), but only the last-created control effect will determine who controls the opponent’s next actual turn, so you control that single next turn only. See [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14] and [500.7]. • If the targeted player skips their next turn, the control effect applies to the next turn that player actually takes, and the extra turn(s) are taken after that turn (see [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #16]).

Timing note (assumption): I assumed the cast trigger from Emrakul, the Promised End and the copy of that trigger are on the stack when you use Lithoform Engine to make a copy of the Emrakul, the Promised End spell. The core conclusions don’t change if the copied permanent spell resolves before the triggers resolve: the copy-of-spell is not cast (no cast trigger), it becomes a token when it resolves ([707.10], [111.13], [Lithoform Engine ruling #6]), and the two trigger instances still produce the control/extra-turn effects as described when they resolve.

TLDR: You control only one of that opponent’s turns (their next turn); you get a token Emrakul, the Promised End when the copied permanent spell resolves; and copying the Emrakul, the Promised End spell does not produce another cast trigger.

results.question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
results.text: Yes — you can get two tokens, assuming a card is exiled with Mimic Vat when each instance of the ability resolves. Lithoform Engine’s first ability copies an activated ability on the stack and puts another instance of that ability on the stack (Lithoform Engine ruling #3). A copy of an ability is itself an ability on the stack and the copy has the same source as the original ability (707.10b; Lithoform Engine ruling #0). Therefore activating Mimic Vat’s {3},{T} ability and then copying that ability with Lithoform Engine creates two separate instances of Mimic Vat’s activated ability on the stack. Each resolving instance will create “a token that’s a copy of a card exiled with Mimic Vat” using whatever card is exiled with Mimic Vat at the time that instance resolves (Mimic Vat ruling #4). You may activate Mimic Vat’s ability even if no card is exiled with Mimic Vat, but if no card is exiled with Mimic Vat by the time an instance resolves, that instance won’t create a token (Mimic Vat ruling #6; 111.12). As a result, the interaction can produce zero, one, or two tokens depending on whether a card is exiled with Mimic Vat at the times the two instances resolve, and the two tokens could be copies of different cards if the exiled card changes between resolutions (Mimic Vat ruling #4).

results.question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
results.text:
Direct answer: If you announce X = 0 for Awaken the Woods, the locked-in total cost will be {1}{G}{G} and you’ll create 0 tokens. For value, you should choose X ≥ 1 (pick as large an X as you can actually pay) so you get at least one 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature token for the same or little extra mana.

Why: X is a placeholder that you must choose and announce as part of casting the spell (107.3a, 601.2b). Awaken the Woods’s mana cost is {X}{G}{G} and its effect is “Create X 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens” (Awaken the Woods). To determine the total cost you start with the mana cost you’re paying, apply any cost increases and then any cost reductions, and finally apply Trinisphere’s effect if the spell’s mana component is less than three (Total Cost; 601.2f; [Trinisphere ruling #0]).

Example with the described cost-reduction permanent that reduces the spell’s mana cost by {1} (applied as a cost reduction before Trinisphere, per the cost-determination order above):
- If you announce X = 0, the mana cost before reductions is {G}{G}. After the {1}-off reduction there’s no generic portion to reduce, so it stays {G}{G}. Trinisphere then makes any spell whose mana component is less than three cost three mana, so the locked-in total cost becomes {1}{G}{G}. You pay {1}{G}{G} and create 0 tokens (Awaken the Woods; [Trinisphere ruling #0]; Total Cost).
- If you announce X = 1, the mana cost before reductions is {1}{G}{G}. Apply the {1}-off reduction and the generic {1} becomes 0, so it would be {G}{G}; Trinisphere then raises the mana component to three, making the locked-in total cost {1}{G}{G} again. You pay {1}{G}{G} and create 1 token. So choosing X = 1 is strictly better than choosing X = 0 in that situation.

Therefore, because Trinisphere forces the spell’s locked-in mana payment to be at least three, you’re already paying that baseline—so don’t set X = 0 and waste it; announce X ≥ 1 (as large as your available mana allows) when you cast Awaken the Woods (107.3a; 601.2b; Awaken the Woods; [Trinisphere ruling #0]; Total Cost).

results.question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
results.text:
Yes. You can target and return Grist, the Hunger Tide from your graveyard with Animate Dead, but Animate Dead won’t be able to remain attached and will end up in your graveyard while Grist, the Hunger Tide stays on the battlefield as a planeswalker (not a creature).

Why: 
- Grist, the Hunger Tide is a creature card while it’s in your graveyard, so it’s a legal target for Animate Dead’s “enchant creature card in a graveyard” (see Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1 and Animate Dead’s enchant ability) [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1, Animate Dead].
- When Animate Dead enters the battlefield, it returns the enchanted creature card to the battlefield and then attempts to attach itself to that new object (Animate Dead ruling #1). Moving the card from the graveyard to the battlefield makes it a new object (rule 400.7), and Grist, the Hunger Tide becomes a planeswalker on the battlefield rather than a creature (Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1).  
- Because Grist, the Hunger Tide is not a creature on the battlefield, Animate Dead can’t legally enchant it. If the returned permanent can’t be legally enchanted by Animate Dead, Animate Dead won’t be able to attach and is put into its owner’s graveyard as a state-based action; that causes Animate Dead’s delayed triggered ability to trigger (Animate Dead ruling #4). When that delayed trigger resolves it says to sacrifice “the creature” if it’s still on the battlefield—but Grist, the Hunger Tide is not a creature on the battlefield, so that condition is false and you don’t sacrifice Grist, the Hunger Tide (Animate Dead ruling #4, Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1). 

Result: Grist, the Hunger Tide ends up on the battlefield under your control as a planeswalker (with whatever loyalty it enters with). Animate Dead ends up in your graveyard and never remains attached to Grist, the Hunger Tide, so its -1/-0 effect and the “when this Aura leaves…” sacrifice interaction don’t cause Grist, the Hunger Tide to be sacrificed.

Assumption: I’m assuming the normal sequence of Animate Dead entering and resolving in the way described by its rulings; if Animate Dead isn’t on the battlefield when its triggered effect would resolve, its return effect simply won’t happen (Animate Dead ruling #0). This answer does not change depending on number of players.

results.question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
results.text:
Yes. Skullbriar, the Walking Grave keeps the four +1/+1 counters when it goes to the command zone and those counters are still on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave when you recast it, but Doubling Season does not double those retained counters as it re-enters the battlefield.

Reasoning and definitions

- Definition (key terms): "Counters that remain/are retained" means counters that the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card keeps on it as it changes zones rather than being removed and then "put" on the new object. "Put/placed" on a permanent means an effect explicitly puts counters onto that permanent (the sort of event Doubling Season modifies).

- Normally, counters don’t survive a zone change and an object that moves zones becomes a new object (rules: counters cease to exist on zone change [122.2]; an object that moves becomes a new object [400.7]).

- Skullbriar, the Walking Grave’s own text specifically says counters remain on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave as it moves to any zone other than a player’s hand or library, so the card’s text causes the counters to be retained when it’s put into the command zone after it dies (this is why your Skullbriar, the Walking Grave keeps its four +1/+1 counters in the command zone). The commander-specific rule allowing a commander to be put into the command zone applies here (see [903.9a]). See the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card data and rulings for this behavior.

- Doubling Season doubles counters that are put on a permanent or doubles permanents that enter with counters in the cases it applies to. However, the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2 explains that the counters that "remain" on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave as it changes zones aren’t considered to have been "placed" on it, and effects like Doubling Season won’t affect those retained counters. Therefore Doubling Season does not double the counters that Skullbriar, the Walking Grave carried through the command zone when it re-enters the battlefield.

Short note on edge cases

- If Skullbriar, the Walking Grave were to go to a player’s hand or library, its printed text says counters do not remain in those cases, so the counters would cease to exist. (The above answer assumes the move was to the command zone, as you stated.)

results.question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
results.text: No — you won’t lose the game. Final Fortune’s “At the beginning of that turn’s end step, you lose the game” triggered ability won’t get a chance to trigger if you use Sundial of the Infinite to end the extra turn before its end step begins, because ending the turn this way skips the end step entirely. Definition: “End the turn” means to perform an expedited process that skips almost everything else that would happen that turn (see rule 724 and the End the Turn description). Reasoning: Sundial of the Infinite’s ability “End the turn” causes the current phase/step to end and skips straight to the cleanup step, with the end step skipped and no “at the beginning of the end step” triggers occurring that turn [Sundial of the Infinite ruling #4; 724.1d]. Sundial of the Infinite’s rulings explicitly state that if its ability is activated before the end step, any “at the beginning of the end step”-triggered abilities won’t get the chance to trigger that turn [Sundial of the Infinite ruling #1], and Final Fortune’s ruling confirms that if you end up skipping the extra turn that is gained, you do not lose the game [Final Fortune ruling #1]. Timing assumption: this answer assumes you activate Sundial of the Infinite before the extra turn’s end step begins. If instead you activate Sundial of the Infinite after the extra turn’s end step has already begun, that “at the beginning of the end step” trigger would already have occurred and you would lose the game (a step that has already started can’t be skipped) [614.10a].

results.question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
results.text: You choose what Clone copies as Clone is entering the battlefield — that choice is made by Clone’s controller as Clone’s “enter as a copy” effect is applied, and opponents do not get to respond to that choice. Reasoning: Clone’s ability is an “as this enters” choice that the controller of Clone makes for the object as it enters the battlefield ([707.6], [707.5]). Because Clone becomes a copy as it enters (it doesn’t enter and then become a copy), there is no point between making that choice and the object having entered when players get priority to respond with spells or activated abilities ([707.5]). Clone’s ability doesn’t target, so you may choose any creature already on the battlefield (you may not choose a creature that is entering at the same time) ([Clone ruling #0], [Clone ruling #2]). If multiple replacement effects try to modify how Clone would enter, the affected object’s controller chooses which replacement effect to apply (APNAP order applies if multiple players choose) ([616.1c]). I’m assuming a normal single-player choice by Clone’s controller as Clone is entering; the answer is the same in multiplayer except that if multiple replacement effects are available, APNAP order governs who chooses among them ([616.1c]).

results.question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
results.text:
You get three lands. The original Flooded Strand ability plus two copies each resolve and each put a Plains or Island onto the battlefield.

Reasoning and definitions (short): "To copy a spell, activated ability, or triggered ability" means to put a copy of it onto the stack; a copy of an activated ability isn’t activated and is itself an ability on the stack (707.10b). You activated Flooded Strand’s ability first, paying its costs (including tapping and sacrificing Flooded Strand); that put the Flooded Strand activated ability on the stack. You then activated Gogo, Master of Mimicry with X=2. When Gogo, Master of Mimicry’s ability resolves it creates two additional instances (copies) of the Flooded Strand activated ability on the stack (Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #6). Each copy is a copy of that activated ability and will, when it resolves, do what the original ability does (707.10b). The source of each copy is the same as the source of the original ability (Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #9), and the copies use the same objects used to pay the original ability’s costs if the effect refers to those objects (707.10b). Altogether the original Flooded Strand activated ability and the two copies resolve (three resolutions), producing three lands entering the battlefield.

If you meant a different timing/order (for example, if you activated Gogo, Master of Mimicry before activating Flooded Strand), say so and I’ll explain that scenario.

results.question: I'm attacking with [Stampeding Rhino] and my opponent blocks with [Vampire Nighthawk]. How much combat damage do I have to assign to the blocker before I can trample the rest over to my opponent?
results.text: You must assign 3 damage from Stampeding Rhino to Vampire Nighthawk before you can assign any of the remaining 1 damage from Stampeding Rhino to the defending player. Reasoning: Stampeding Rhino is a 4/4 and thus assigns 4 combat damage (see rule 510.1a). Trample requires an attacking creature to assign lethal damage to the creatures blocking it before any excess may be assigned to the player (see rule 702.19b). Vampire Nighthawk has toughness 3, so lethal damage for Vampire Nighthawk is 3 (see rule 120.4a). Stampeding Rhino does not have deathtouch; the deathtouch ability on Vampire Nighthawk only makes damage dealt by a source with deathtouch count as lethal for that source (see rule 702.2c and the Vampire Nighthawk card text), which does not reduce the amount Stampeding Rhino must assign. Therefore Stampeding Rhino must be assigned at least 3 damage to Vampire Nighthawk and the remaining 1 damage may be assigned to the defending player.
